after.authors: El Jamal, N.; Brooks, T. G.; Penn Medicine Biobank,  ; Skarke, C.; FitzGerald, G. A.
after.abstract: Background. Anthracyclines are widely used chemotherapeutics limited by dose-dependent cardiotoxicity. Because cardiovascular physiology and drug handling oscillate across the day, the timing of drug administration may influence cardiac risk. Optimal timing may depend on both an individual's internal circadian phase and environmental light exposure. We tested whether dosing time is associated with anthracycline cardiotoxicity, whether this is also true of overall treatment outcomes, and whether optimal dosing time is modified by photoperiod and the genetically predicted chronotype. Methods. We analyzed ejection fraction (EF) change following anthracycline exposure in the All of Us research program (AoU; 70 patients) and incident heart failure (HF) in the Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; 843 patients). Dosing time was modeled on both clock-time and solar (time-from-sunrise) axes using flexible splines, with likelihood-ratio tests (LRT) for association and for interaction with photoperiod and a germline chronotype polygenic score (cPGS). The cPGS was validated against wearable-derived midsleep and heart-rate rhythms. Results. Dosing time was associated with anthracycline cardiotoxicity in both cohorts, with greater harm at later dosing times (AoU EF LRT p=0.011 clock, p=0.029 sunrise; PMBB HF p=0.052 sunrise, p=0.084 clock). No association was observed with non-HF mortality (p=0.75, 0.77), consistent with a narrowing of the therapeutic index. Photoperiod modified the dosing-time association (AoU p=0.064 clock, p=0.062 sunrise; PMBB p=0.023 clock, p=0.093 sunrise). Modification by cPGS was directionally consistent across cohorts but did not reach significance, likely reflecting attenuation of a polygenic proxy capturing limited chronotype variance. Conclusions. Anthracycline dosing time is associated with cardiotoxicity but not mortality and is modified by photoperiod, identifying dosing time as a modifiable, circadian-sensitive factor. These findings motivate prospective, chronotype- and season-informed studies of anthracycline scheduling.

after.authors: Hup, R. G.; Kortman, M. E.; Kuijpers, R. W. F. H.; Mensinck, M. J. S.; Bouchnaf, C.; Ouss, A. J.; Tan, H. L.; Haakma, R.; Dekker, L. R. C.; Long, X.; Vullings, R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Electrical Engineering, Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, The Netherlands
after.abstract: Objective. Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is often unwitnessed, which delays treatment and lowers the chance of survival. A smartwatch could act as a witness by detecting loss of pulse from wrist photoplethysmography (PPG) and subsequently alert emergency services. We aimed to develop and evaluate such a detection model. Approach. As smartwatch data of OHCA are extremely difficult to acquire, we used in-hospital proxy data to test sensitivity: wrist PPG and accelerometry recorded during baseline and induced loss-of-pulse periods in 31 patients during catheter ablation of ventricular arrhythmias and defibrillation threshold (DFT) testing during subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) implantation (BECA-S2). In total, 33 loss-of-pulse events, annotated using accompanying electrocardiograms and, where available, arterial blood pressure, were included. To count false alarms, we used wrist PPG and accelerometry of 100 healthy volunteers during unsupervised daily activities (BECA-S6). A recurrent neural network was evaluated with cross-validation, with one fold per patient with events. As the electrical VF induction and defibrillation shocks applied during these procedures would not be present in true OHCA episodes, we tested for and mitigated the resulting target leakage. Main results. The Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC) was 86.8% (95% CI: 79.7 to 92.5%) and the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (PR-AUC) was 52.4% (95% CI: 38.6 to 66.2%). At a false alarm rate of zero on BECA-S6, the event-level sensitivity on BECA-S2 was 48.5% (95% CI: 32.1 to 65.5%). Higher sensitivities came at the cost of more false alarms. Without mitigation, target leakage inflated the model scores by 35.3% (95% CI: 11.5 to 61.4%) of the model's discriminative range. Significance. These results show the feasibility of smartwatch-based loss-of-pulse detection. Larger studies with data more representative of OHCA are needed. We recommend that future studies on induced loss of pulse test for and mitigate target leakage.

after.authors: Rajkumar, J.; Manjunath, S.; Makan, M.; Moreno, J.; Davis, J.; May, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Medicine, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO
after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Standard echocardiographic metrics of diastolic function assess ventricular relaxation and filling pressures largely independent of systolic performance. OBJECTIVES: To introduce and evaluate the Cardiac Efficiency Index (CEI), a novel echocardiographic parameter integrating mitral inflow kinetics with forward stroke volume to provide a more integrated assessment of diastolic physiology. METHODS: We convenience sampled 82 patients with recent transthoracic echocardiography. CEI was evaluated against American Society of Echocardiography (ASE) diastolic dysfunction (DD) grade and left atrial pressure (LAP; normal or elevated). Binary logistic regression evaluated discrimination of elevated LAP and ASE grade [≥]2. Ordinal logistic regression evaluated increasing ASE grade (0-1, 2, 3). RESULTS: Elevated LAP was present in 33/80 (41.3%) patients with valid assessment while 22/66 (33.3%) patients with valid ASE grading had grade [≥]2 DD. For elevated LAP, CEI yielded an AUROC of 0.954 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.898-0.993] compared with 0.949 [0.895-0.988] for E/e'. For ASE grade [≥]2 AUROC was 0.941 [0.854-0.994] for CEI and 0.942 [0.868-0.991] for E/e'. Ordinal regression demonstrated comparable discrimination (c-index 0.904 [CEI] vs. 0.912 [E/e']) while CEI had a larger per-SD association with increasing ASE grade (OR 10.45 [4.03-27.08]) than E/e' (OR 7.58 [2.92-19.67]). In the combined model, CEI remained independently associated with increasing ASE grade (OR 6.82 [2.24-20.73]; P<0.001) whereas E/e' did not (OR 1.75 [0.70-4.38]; P=0.23). CONCLUSIONS: CEI provided strong discrimination of elevated LAP and ASE DD grade in this proof-of-concept analysis, supporting further validation against invasive hemodynamics in larger cohorts.

after.authors: Rees, N.; Todd, D.; Williams, L.; O'Meara, P.; Williams, J.; Hawkes, C.
after.abstract: Background Violence and aggression (V&A) occurs in approximate 4-5% of Emergency Medical Services (EMS) calls. EMS staff endure many forms of V&A including verbal threats, physical injury, sexual assaults and on rare occasions fatalities occur. This can result in stress, fear, anxiety, and burnout in EMS staff, and there is significant interest in tacking this issue. Few evidence-based interventions exist, and despite their importance, public attitudes are notably missing in this discourse. This paper presents findings of a qualitative content analysis of free text survey responses to a survey of Wales (UK) adult attitudes towards V&A directed towards EMS staff. Methods Two independent samples of online YouGov surveys of Wales adults conducted in 2022 and 2024 were combined and qualitative content analysis conducted of the free text narrative responses. Results Two thousand and fourteen narrative responses were analysed, and the following conceptual themes emerged: -Multimodal, cumulative and confabulated knowing -Dual discourse of V&A directed towards EMS staff Conclusion The public overwhelmingly reported disgust at V&A towards EMS staff and appear to recognise the complexity of this issue. Whilst responses reflect efforts aimed at tackling this issue, including media campaigns and legislation such as the Assaults on Emergency Workers (Offences) Act (2018), we found limited awareness of the actual legislation and media campaigns. Rather, public attitudes appear to be influenced through multimodal and cumulative processes including social interaction, personal views and reflection. We found support for prosecution and harsh criminal sentences for perpetrators of V&A towards EMS staff which aligns to retributivist perspectives and suggests public policy may be aligned with societal and moral expectation. We found limited evidence however for the preventative capacity of current approaches, which is consistent with our previous findings and wider body of knowledge. We therefore call for future research and policy to focus on the complexity and dual discourse revealed in this and other studies and follow consequentialist approaches to tackling these issues to prevent future V&A, reduce recidivism, and promote safety.

after.abstract: Background Envenoming by krait (Genus: Bungarus) that are widespread through Asia results in over 10,000 deaths annually in India alone. Krait venoms contain presynaptic secretory phospholipase A2 (sPLA2) neurotoxins that target motor nerve terminals and impair acetylcholine release. The resulting flaccid paralysis may progress rapidly leading to airway compromise, respiratory failure and death. Varespladib, an investigational small-molecule inhibitor of sPLA2, has demonstrated rescue efficacy against lethal krait envenoming in animal models. Methods We report a subgroup analysis of patients with krait envenoming enrolled in BRAVIO, a multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted in India and the U.S. Patients received intravenous followed by oral varespladib or placebo, in addition to standard-of-care antivenom. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05717062) and Clinical Trials Registry-India (CTRI/2023/10/058782). Findings The efficacy analysis included 45 (24 varespladib, 21 placebo) of the 46 randomized patients. The prespecified primary endpoint was time to recovery of 5-second head lift. The mean time was 27.6 hours for varespladib vs 36.2 hours for placebo, difference -8.6 hours, 95% CI -38.3 to 21.1. Illness severity over the first week, measured using area under the curve for the Snakebite Severity Score through Day 7, was lower in the varespladib group (296 vs 464; difference -168, 95% CI -279 to -57.6). Varespladib patients showed a greater early reduction in Snakebite Severity Score over the first six hours than placebo (difference 1.5, 95% CI 0.5 to 2.5). Among intubated, mechanically ventilated patients (n=25), median duration of intubation was 14.9 hours (IQR 11.5 to 23.3) in the varespladib group versus 34.0 hours (IQR 28.0 to 45.0) in the placebo group. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in seven varespladib-treated and six placebo-treated patients (29% each for both groups). Interpretation The consistent findings of earlier neuromuscular improvement, lower illness severity, and shorter duration of intubation suggest that adjunctive varespladib accelerates recovery from severe neurotoxic krait envenoming.

Varespladib patients showed a greater early reduction in Snakebite Severity Score over the first six hours than placebo (difference 1.5, 95% CI 0.5 to 2.5). after.abstract: Background: The World Health Organization conditionally recommends mass drug administration (MDA) for short-term reductions in malaria burden, including in emergencies. We assessed the association of a time-limited MDA and indoor residual spraying (IRS) campaign with malaria prevalence and mortality up to 14 months after its last MDA round in Angumu, a malaria holoendemic and conflict-affected health zone in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Methods: Fourteen health areas were allocated non-randomly to MDA+IRS (those with the highest malaria incidence), IRS alone (those with the least MSF support for case management), or routine care (Routine). Malaria prevalence by rapid diagnostic test was measured at 0, 7, 13, 18, and 24 months from March 2022, and under-five and crude mortality at 0, 13, and 24 months. Within each survey, zones were compared by mixed-effects regression adjusted for area-level baseline values and individual displacement status. Routine areas were excluded after receiving interventions, leaving one at 24 months. Results: At every later survey, the odds of malaria in the MDA+IRS zone were approximately a quarter to a third of those in the Routine zone. This difference persisted to the last survey, 14 months after the last MDA round, with prevalence of 24.4% compared with 56.4% (odds ratio [OR] 0.31, 95% CI 0.19-0.50). IRS alone was associated with lower prevalence during the campaign, but not statistically significantly afterwards. Prevalence was lower in the MDA+IRS than in the IRS zone at 18 and 24 months (ORs 0.37 and 0.47); during the campaign, the difference was not statistically significant after adjustment for baseline prevalence. Mortality differences were not statistically significant, except lower crude mortality in the MDA+IRS than the Routine zone at 13 months. In 2023, the sporozoite rate was lower in the intervention zones than the Routine zone, and facility test positivity was lowest in the MDA+IRS zone at every later survey. Conclusions: In holoendemic, conflict-affected settings, malaria programmes and humanitarian organisations may consider co-timed MDA and IRS where high coverage is achievable, with prevalence monitored in repeated surveys to decide when to repeat the campaign.

after.authors: Wang, L.; Brown, J. L.; Sun, D.; Xi, N. M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Statistics, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana
after.abstract: Drug use at discharge from substance use treatment is a national outcome measure that the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration computes for state block grant performance tables. Researchers analyze it in the public-use files of the Treatment Episode Data Set Discharges (TEDS-D). The federal specification codes the frequency of use for a "None" substance as not applicable. We examined how the TEDS-D public-use files for 2015 to 2024 code these records. From 2018 to 2024, every public-use record with "None" as the primary discharge substance had its frequency coded as missing or unknown. We call such records with no other discharge substance all-None records. All-None records were 12.5% of discharges in 2024. Among 729,346 discharges from 2018 to 2024 of adults admitted with daily use of heroin, other opioids, methamphetamine, or cocaine who stayed at least 31 days and did not die in treatment, 64,821 (8.9%) were all-None records. Massachusetts and New Jersey, whose discharge forms document "None" as reported no use, contributed 81.7% of them. With all-None records dropped, New Jersey's rate of no use at discharge was 6.8% (49th of 51 jurisdictions). Counting them as no use raised it to 52% (18th). A 2021 reporting change in Massachusetts implied that 98% (95% CI, 97% to 99%) of its all-None records reported no use. In 2024, New Jersey's block grant table reported 98.9% abstinence at discharge in short-term residential treatment among clients who used drugs at admission. The public-use frequency field gave 14.7%. Counting "None" as no use reproduced the federal values within 4.1 percentage points in every setting and year. A published national analysis excluded 93.9% of completed episodes in New Jersey. Of these, 95.2% were all-None records. Analyses that define use from the frequency field drop documented reports of no use in New Jersey and Massachusetts.

D.; Saini, T.; Chan, A.; Columbo, L.; Horgan, J.; Newell-Rogers, M. K.; Blish, C. A.; Lewis, D. B.; Maecker, H.; Frankovich, J.
after.abstract: Importance: Pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS) lacks validated disease-activity biomarkers. Relationships between peripheral immune-cell activation and psychiatric severity remain incompletely characterized. Objective: To compare peripheral immune-cell phenotypes during PANS flare and recovery with those of healthy controls and evaluate associations with psychiatric severity and functional impairment. Design, Setting, and Participants: In this prospective single-center cohort study, peripheral blood and psychiatric symptom ratings were collected from 20 patients meeting PANS criteria and 20 matched healthy controls at Stanford University Immune Behavioral Health Program between November 2016 to January 2020. Main Predictors: Clinical group (PANS flare, PANS recovery, or healthy control) and peripheral B-cell, CD4+ T-cell, monocyte, and NK-cell ratios. Main Outcomes and Measures: Mass cytometry quantified ratios of activated (CD19+CD20+CD69+) to naive (CD19+CD20+IgD+CD27-) B-cells; activated (CD3+CD4+CD69+) to naive (CD3+CD4+CD45RA+CD27+) T-cells; classical (CD14+CD16-CCR2+) to nonclassical/patrolling (CD14+CD16+CX3CR1+) monocytes; and activated (CD56-bright CD69+) to resting (CD56-dim) NK cells. Primary clinical measures were the clinician-rated Childrens Global Assessment Scale (CGAS), parent-rated PANS Global Impairment Scale, and PANS-31 Symptom Rating Scale (30 available items). Linear mixed-effects models accounted for repeated measurements; false discovery rate (FDR) correction addressed multiple testing. Results: Analyses included 19 flare samples, 15 recovery samples, and 20 healthy control samples. B-cell, CD4+ T-cell, monocyte, and NK-cell activation ratios were higher during flare than in healthy controls (all P < .01) or recovery (all P < .03). Recovery and control ratios did not differ significantly. Each one unit increase in the B-cell activation ratio was associated with lower CGAS scores, indicating worse functioning (Beta = -14.89; FDR-adjusted P < .001), higher Global Impairment scores (Beta = 12.81; FDR-adjusted P = .004), and higher PANS-31 scores (Beta = 8.37; FDR-adjusted P = .012). CD4+ T-cell, monocyte, and NK-cell activation ratios were not significantly associated with psychiatric scores. Adjustment for sex or immunomodulatory medication exposure did not materially alter B-cell associations. Adjustment for disease state attenuated these associations, although the CGAS association remained significant. Conclusions and Relevance: In this longitudinal observational study, PANS flares were associated with higher peripheral immune-cell activation ratios across all cell subsets studies (B, CD4+ T, monocyte, and NK). Only B-cell activation ratios were associated with greater psychiatric severity and impairment. The activated-to-naive B-cell ratio warrants independent validation as a candidate disease-activity marker for the psychiatric aspects of PANS; these findings do not establish causality or clinical utility.

after.authors: Grover, E. N.; Hill, A.; Gunn, E. J.; DeVoss, R.; Liang, R.; Jolley, S. E.; Perraillon, M. C.; Carlton, E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Environmental and Occupational Health, Colorado School of Public Health, University of Colorado Anschutz
after.abstract: Background: Long COVID (LC) is a complex, multisystemic condition whose prevalence is poorly understood due, in part, to underdiagnosis. Methods: We used the Colorado All Payer Claims Database (CO APCD), which covers approximately 70% of insured Coloradans, to train a machine learning eXtreme Gradient Boosting model to predict undiagnosed LC. The 243 candidate predictors included clinical symptoms, comorbid conditions, healthcare utilization, pharmaceutical prescriptions, and individual- and neighborhood-level socioeconomic conditions. Models were trained on a dataset of 38,064 adults (18+), including individuals with the LC diagnostic code (U09.9), and a set of comparators without the code, matched by age, sex and payer. The trained model was used to estimate the prevalence of undiagnosed LC within a larger CO APCD extract comprising 2.1 million adults. We compared diagnostic patterns across sociodemographic and geographic characteristics by calculating the ratio of predicted undiagnosed to diagnosed prevalence. Results: The prevalence of undiagnosed adult LC in Colorado was estimated to be 8%, corresponding with an estimated 7 undiagnosed cases for every 1 diagnosed case. High levels of healthcare utilization and respiratory-related symptoms were top predictors of LC. Conditions that helped to rule out LC (e.g., musculoskeletal pain) were also important to model performance. Groups with higher proportions of probable, undiagnosed LC relative to diagnosed LC include younger adults, males, and urban populations. Conclusions: Leveraging medical claims, neighborhood socioeconomic and geographic data in advanced machine learning algorithms can facilitate rapid estimation of the hidden burden of undiagnosed LC and identify populations less likely to receive a diagnosis.

after.title: Preprint: Proteogenomic analysis provides insights into the effect of physical activity on cancers
after.authors: Song, A.; Chatterjee, C.; Moore, S. C.; Dutta, D.
after.abstract: Background. Increased physical activity (PA) has been associated with decreased risk of several cancers in epidemiologic studies, but the intermediate molecular mechanisms remains poorly characterized. Methods. Leveraging genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics for 22 self-reported and accelerometer-based PA measures, plasma levels of 2,940 proteins (N = 34,557), and multiple site-specific cancers, we performed a two-stage proteome-wide Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis. In Stage 1, we estimated the effects of each PA measure on plasma protein levels and in Stage 2, we evaluated the effects of PA-associated proteins on cancer risk. Results. We identified 687 PA-protein associations involving 503 unique proteins at FDR<0.05. Across 80 PA-responsive proteins curated from intervention-based studies, we nominally replicated 83% using our MR approach. Approximately 40% of PA-associated proteins were differentially expressed in response to exercise in transcriptomic datasets primarily localizing to muscle tissues, and in immune cell populations. In stage 2, 213 (of 503) PA-related proteins demonstrated significant effects on at least one cancer (FDR<0.05) highlighting them as proteomic intermediates of the effect of PA on cancer. For example, for prostate cancer (PCa), we observed that reductions in sedentary time and increases in light-intensity activity were associated with higher MSMB and lower TNF levels, which in turn reduced PCa risk. Conclusions. This study applies a two-stage Mendelian randomization framework to link PA, circulating proteins, and cancer risk, enhancing biological interpretation of epidemiologic PA-cancer associations and nominating a focused set of PA-associated proteins as potential targets for further investigation.

after.title: Preprint: Facilitators for green behaviour change during GP consultations: a qualitative study
after.authors: Visser, E. H.; Koivusaari, S.; Slootweg, I. A.; Brakema, E. A.; Vos, H. M. M.; Adriaanse, M. A.
after.abstract: Background: GP consultations are a major source of primary care's environmental impact and therefore a promising point of intervention for mitigation. Understanding how pioneers, green GPs, have successfully changed their behaviour during these consultations, may support other GPs to follow suit. Aim: To identify key facilitators for GPs to change their behaviour from environmentally less sustainable to environmentally more sustainable during consultations. Design and setting: In 2025, we conducted a qualitative study with Dutch green GPs, defined as GPs with knowledge of and interest in sustainable healthcare, and who apply sustainable behaviours during consultations. Method: We used semi-structured interviews guided by three vignettes about green behaviour changes: sustainable prescribing of inhalation medication, prescribing less per consultation, and focussing on lifestyle changes before starting preventive cardiovascular medication. We deductively coded the facilitators using the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF), followed by inductive coding using thematic analysis. Results: We interviewed 12 green GPs and found that the key facilitators loaded on the TDF domains: knowledge (fostering moments of realisation), environmental context and resources (a supportive green workplace), social influence (a green network) and beliefs about consequences (focusing on benefits). Conclusion: Changing GPs' behaviour during consultations to be environmentally more sustainable begins with realising the impact of healthcare on the planet, and is sustained by focusing on the benefits of sustainable healthcare and creating opportunities within physical and social environments. Building on these facilitators, interventions should focus on altering care environments to enable GPs to easily opt for the sustainable option.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Center of Eating and feeding Disorder Research, Mental Health Centre Ballerup, Copenhagen University Hospital, Herlev and Gentofte, Denmark
after.abstract: Eating disorders are heritable and comorbid with many psychiatric and somatic conditions, potentially due to shared genetic risk. We investigated associations of genetic liability to anorexia nervosa and binge eating across diverse health-related phenotypes in the UK Biobank. Using PHESANT, we tested associations between SBayes-RC-derived polygenic scores for (1) anorexia nervosa (PGSAN) and (2) binge eating (PGSBE) with 8,657 phenotypes in UK Biobank (N=456,775). Analyses focused on European genetically-inferred ancestry, with secondary analyses examining the role of measured BMI and BMI polygenic scores (PGSBMI), and extending to African, Admixed American, South Asian, and East Asian genetically-inferred ancestry groups. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for sampling weights. PGSAN and PGSBE showed broadly similar associations with psychiatric and psychological vulnerability. However, they diverged across somatic, metabolic, and anthropometric traits, e.g., PGSBE was associated with earlier pubertal timing across female (age at menarche; OR=0.93, 95% CI 0.93, 0.94, p<0.001) and male (e.g., relative age of voice breaking; OR=0.96, 95% CI 0.95, 0.97, p<0.001) markers of puberty, although associations with male markers were attenuated after BMI adjustment. No such associations were observed for PGSAN. Adjusting for BMI and PGSBMI substantially attenuated anthropometric and metabolic associations, particularly for PGSBE. Analyses in non-European ancestry groups identified fewer significant associations, likely reflecting reduced power and poor cross-ancestry transferability of PGS. Adjusting for sampling weights altered effect sizes most for psychiatric and somatic traits, suggesting these associations are particularly susceptible to participation bias. Across the phenome, PGSAN and PGSBE exhibited common psychiatric liability alongside divergent somatic, anthropometric, and metabolic association patterns which reflects clinically observed differences in medical sequelae between the phenotypes.

after.title: Preprint: Ordinal Probit Modeling of Loneliness, Relationship Difficulty, Worthlessness, and Depression in Midlife: An Ordinal Association Analysis of Psychosocial and Demographic Predictors
after.authors: Katuri, G. B.; Pairdha, A. K.
after.abstract: Midlife is a time of significant social, economic, and health change, and the covariation between demographic and psychosocial characteristics and ill-being has both preventional and organisational implications. This is an attempt to produce a single ordinal variable summarising information about mental health- ill-being, and its dependence on demographic predictors. We measure mental ill-being through four midlife-related outcomes: loneliness frequency (RA1SA20G), ability to sustain close relationships (RA1SF1J), worthlessness frequency (RA1SA20F), and degree of depressive symptomatology (RA1PDEPRE), and explore a fifth, anxiety (RA1PANXIE) at the descriptive, but not inferential, level. The predictors are age and sex, pain of financial difficulty in meeting the monthly bills, purposefulness/agentic engagement, self-efficacy, sleep difficulty, contact with social media, meditation/relaxation use, and leisure vigorous activity. After removing missing or refused values (listwise deletion), 2,423 respondents (52.9% female; age range 23 to 76, mean 51.84, SD 14.20) from the initial 3,577 sample extract remain; we give univariate, one-variable summaries, merge sparse categories of the predictor variables through a limited number of theoretically motivated recodes, and establish the strength of association of predictor pairs with ordinal correlation coefficients (Kendall's tau-b, Stuart's tau-c, and rank-biserial correlation for sex). We fit maximum-likelihood ordinal probit models both as models with a sole predictor variable (each in turn) and as a conditional (multi-predictor) model with four predictors (bins of age, bill difficulty, purposefulness/agency, and sleep difficulty) as a function of cross-validated predictive accuracy estimates from stratified five-fold cross-validation. We find high cross-validated predictive accuracy for depression (0.864), and worthlessness (0.808), and lower but still modest predictive accuracy for loneliness (0.653 to 0.655) and the ability to sustain close relationships (0.291 to 0.304); single-predictor accuracy estimates were not improved substantially in the combined models. We discuss how our decisions about recode levels, the interpretation of the ordinal association coefficients, potential limitations of the models and how future predictions could benefit from the inclusion of sample weights, ordinal-loss functions for model assessment, ordinal proportional-odds diagnostics, and model-based causal pathways from longitudinal waves of the MIDUS study.

after.title: Preprint: Depression Measurement in Autistic Adults and Adults Who Did Not Meet Autism Criteria: Retrospective Psychometric Evaluation of the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 in Telehealth Psychotherapy
after.authors: Whaling, K. M.; Olson, L.; Fraley, M.; Jones, H.; Heinly, J.; Mazurek, M.; Loftin, R.
after.abstract: Background: The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) is widely used to measure depressive symptoms, but its performance in autistic adults remains understudied. In autism-focused telehealth care, it is unclear whether PHQ-9 scores can be interpreted similarly for adults who meet autism criteria and those who do not, or across demographic subgroups of autistic adults. Objective: This study evaluated PHQ-9 reliability, internal structure, and associations with anxiety to inform score interpretation in psychotherapy with autistic adults. Total-score comparability and item 9 endorsement were compared between adults who met autism criteria and adults assessed in the same service who did not. An exploratory aim was to assess score comparability across subgroups of diagnosed adults. Methods: This retrospective psychometric study used the first eligible check-in with paired PHQ-9 and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) scores in 2 nonoverlapping cohorts. The original cohort included 3,471 clients diagnosed with autism and 484 who completed the same service's assessment without meeting diagnostic criteria. The replication cohort included 7,406 and 1,194 clients, respectively. Ordinal factor models assessed structure and whether item responses were comparable across groups at the same severity. Graded response models compared expected totals at matched latent severity across all 56 sets of 3 anchor items from items 1-8. Logistic models compared item 9 endorsement (response [≥]1) at matched Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8) scores. Results: Across anchor sets, diagnosed-minus-comparison differences in expected PHQ-9 totals, averaged over latent severity, ranged from -0.46 to 0.35 points in the original cohort and -0.47 to 0.49 points in replication. Model-specific 95% interval endpoints spanned -0.80 to 0.59 and -0.68 to 0.63 points, respectively. The largest upper bounds for the average absolute difference on the 0-27 scale were 0.502 and 0.524 points, respectively. Cronbach's alpha ranged from 0.84 to 0.86. The correlated two-factor model fit better than the one-factor model, though absolute fit remained limited. PHQ-9 and GAD-7 correlations ranged from 0.69 to 0.74. PHQ-9 totals discriminated weakly against recorded depressive-disorder codes (area under the curve 0.60-0.65). In replication, scalar invariance was rejected in the primary comparison, with item-level differences of 0.10 points or less, and in 6 of 7 subgroup contrasts. At PHQ-8=5, the odds ratios for item 9 endorsement were 1.42 (95% CI 0.77-2.61) in the original cohort and 0.66 (95% CI 0.49-0.88) in replication. The joint between-cohort test yielded {chi}^2(2)=5.78, P=.06. Conclusions: The PHQ-9 total appears useful as a group-level summary of depressive symptoms at this service. Average modeled differences were small relative to within-group variation. Item 9 estimates at PHQ-8=5 pointed in opposite directions across cohorts. Comparability with nonautistic adults, diagnostic cutoffs, sensitivity to change, and applicability to other settings and to adults with higher support or different communication needs require further study. after.title: Preprint: Cognitive Trajectories and Clinical Outcomes in the North American Psychosis-Proneness Longitudinal Study (NAPLS2)
after.authors: Yassin, W.; Green, J. B.; Cai, M.; Ansari, D.; Woodbury, K.; Shapiro, D. I.; Allott, K.; He, S.; Kong, X.-J.; Keshavan, M.; Addington, J.; Bearden, C. E.; Cadenhead, K. S.; Cannon, T. D.; Mathalon, D. H.; Perkins, D. O.; Walker, E. F.; Woods, S. W.; Fusar-Poli, P.; Stone, W. S.
after.abstract: Cognitive impairments are well-documented in individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR), particularly among those who convert (i.e., transition) to psychosis. However, considerable heterogeneity in cognitive profiles across CHR populations limits the utility of cognition as a predictive or treatment-relevant marker. This study examined baseline and longitudinal (12 mo and 24 mo) neurocognitive functioning in CHR individuals from the North American Prodrome Longitudinal Study 2 (NAPLS 2) who either transitioned to psychosis or remitted, or who neither converted nor remitted over a 2-year follow-up period. A total of 689 CHR individuals and 265 healthy controls (HC) completed neurocognitive and clinical assessments. CHR participants were categorized based on clinical outcomes: converters (n=89), remitters (n=216), and CHR who neither converted nor remitted (n=384). Group differences at baseline and over time were assessed using ANCOVA and mixed-effects modeling, adjusting for demographic and site-related factors. At baseline, all CHR groups performed worse than HC across nearly all cognitive domains. Subsequent converters showed significantly lower baseline performance than remitters and those who remained CHR throughout the study in key domains, suggestive of state-like effects. All groups, including converters, showed different levels of improvements associated with practice effects. CHR in remission showed cognitive improvements, but not at levels associated with full recovery on most assessments. Our findings suggest that cognitive trajectories within clinical outcome are as heterogenous as those between, suggesting the importance of addressing such differences on a participant level.

after.title: Preprint: Scalable frameworks for local evaluation of AI-enabled imaging devices using PACS-integrated large language models
after.authors: Amurthur, A.; Justice, S. A.; Chin, J. K.; Mercaldo, S. F.; Morley, R. J.; Schultz, A. S.; Silva, V.; Yun, T. J.; Choi, J. W.; Bridge, C. P.; Schultz, T.; Hillis, J. M.
after.abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled imaging device performance may vary across institutions due to differences in disease prevalence, patient demographics, and acquisition protocols. Routine local evaluation, including pre-deployment baseline testing and post-deployment monitoring, remains limited by manual data curation. A large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge approach using existing radiology reports provides a method of performing local evaluation. Methods: We established PACS-integrated LLMs in HIPAA-compliant environments. We then developed two scalable frameworks to automate key processes of local evaluation: selection of a candidate series for device inference and generation of report-derived labels. We applied these frameworks to 4,000 consecutive non-contrast head CT examinations from two hospitals to evaluate agreement between radiology reports and Purple AI Hyper Insight-ICH, a commercial intracranial hemorrhage detection device. Results: For series selection, we used a three-tiered, traffic-light approach across 31,422 available series to select a single series for device inference in 3,976 examinations. For radiology report field extraction, we refined an LLM prompt with three steps: initial binary classification, characterization of discordance between the binary classification prompt output and device output, and a comprehensive prompt (featuring 28 structured fields that were informed by the preceding stages). The positive percent agreement (PPA) depended on the definition of positive cases based on the comprehensive prompt fields: it was 87.7% (79.2 to 95.0%) using similar criteria to many published studies (acute or acute-on-chronic, non-minimal, non-equivocal hemorrhage), yet was lower when including chronic, minimal or equivocal ICH. The negative percent agreement (NPA) was 94.7% (94.0 to 95.4%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated that discrepancies involving a positive device output commonly occurred in the setting of recent intracranial surgery and intracranial hyperdense (non-hemorrhagic) lesions. Conclusion: A PACS-integrated LLM approach, together with scalable frameworks for series selection and label generation, can provide radiologists with local insights about AI-enabled device performance. These insights may help radiologists interpret device outputs in clinical practice, particularly in scenarios associated with greater device-report discordance.

after.title: Preprint: Cascading Feature Refinement with Channel-Wise Attention for Super-Resolution of Gastrointestinal Capsule Endoscopy
after.authors: Katuri, G. B.; Pairdha, A. K.
after.abstract: Wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) now enables endoscopic examination of the whole small bowel, albeit typically in a non-invasive, more comfortable, and generally painless manner. The physical limitations of such endoscopy technology (specifically, sensor array size, battery, and light constraints) usually dictate relatively low-resolution (LR) output video frames. Consequently, capturing, and thus detecting, fine or non-protruding gastrointestinal (GI) abnormalities (e.g., small mucosal vascular lesions, mild angioectasias, and early mucosal neoplastic conditions) can sometimes be clinically sub-optimal. This paper presents a novel cascading feature refinement network involving Dense Shortcut Connections and Channel-wise Attention Mechanism (CFR-CA). The network operates on only the Luminance (Y) component of YCbCr colour space of the WCE images, exploiting high-frequency structures that are key to the GI diagnosis, while efficiently skipping processing steps on Chrominance (Cb, Cr) channels. We collected a dataset of 10,000 WCE frames from different institutions, pre-processing them by manually removing the frame corners to create our training dataset. We utilised bicubic down-sampling (x4) to generate our LR and high-resolution (HR) pairs. Experimental results show that CFR-CA achieves the best RGB Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), the best Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) on both the Y and RGB channels, and the best Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) among contemporary techniques such as SRGAN, DenseNet and RCAN, although its Y channel PSNR remains slightly below those of DenseNet and RCAN. This is expected to aid the efficacy of future CADx models, ultimately helping clinicians to accurately identify GI pathologies in WCE in a more confident and timely manner.

However, real-world application is hindered by inappropriate prescribing and low patient adherence. This study focuses on developing the ACCEPT Decision Intervention (ADI), a tool designed to enhance both physician prescribing and patient adherence in line with clinical guidelines. Methods: The ADI, which incorporates both physician and patient components, was developed using the Knowledge to Action framework. The physician component integrates the Acute COPD Exacerbation Prediction Tool (ACCEPT), a risk scoring tool for exacerbations, into the electronic medical record, offering tailored treatment recommendations based on clinical outcomes. The patient component provides a personalized educational handout addressing medication information, inhaler techniques, and self-management strategies. Development was informed by a series of semi-structured interviews and surveys with pulmonologists and patients, with iterative prototyping based on feedback. Results: Interviews revealed barriers such as physicians' difficulty in risk assessment and patients' misconceptions about medication, which were addressed in the ADI design. The physician tool simplifies guideline adherence by automating risk prediction, while the patient handout offers customized, accessible information to improve treatment adherence. Feedback from pulmonologists highlighted the importance of minimizing workflow disruption, leading to streamlined tool design. Cognitive interviews with patients resulted in revisions to enhance clarity and engagement, such as incorporating more visuals and simplified language. Conclusion: The ADI is a comprehensive, user-centered decision support tool aimed at improving COPD management by communicating exacerbation risk and aligning physician prescribing with guidelines and empowering patients to adhere to treatment. By integrating multivariable risk scoring and behaviour change strategies, this intervention has the potential to reduce exacerbation rates and hospitalizations. Ongoing evaluation in the IMPACT trial will assess its clinical effectiveness and implementation feasibility.

after.title: Preprint: Development and Pilot Implementation of a Classification for Hemodialysis Cannulation Infiltrations: A Single-Center Quality Improvement Study
after.authors: Niyyar, V. D.; Rawls, F.; Broxton-Key, R.; Jones, D. F.
after.abstract: Background: Cannulation-related complications, including infiltrations, are inconsistently defined and documented, making it difficult to establish reliable baselines and compare cannulation techniques and technologies, and assess improvements in care. Further, existing classifications do not systematically capture downstream clinical consequences. Methods: To address these gaps, we developed a novel grading classification for infiltrations, combining immediate local injury severity with modifiers for downstream clinical consequences. The classification was piloted in a quality improvement project at Emory outpatient hemodialysis units from July 1 through September 30, 2026. All infiltrations during the study period were recorded and assigned both severity grades and clinical modifiers; management and follow-up were summarized descriptively. Results: Among 12 reported infiltrations, seven were recorded as Grade 1, three as Grade 2, and two as Grade 3. Dialysis was disrupted in 11 treatments, with access rest required in 9 patients. In 6 instances, a pre-existing central venous catheter was used until the arteriovenous access was able to be successfully reused. Conclusions: The classification supports systematic documentation of infiltration severity and clinically relevant consequences, providing a starting point for establishing baselines and tracking cannulation outcomes. Further refinement and validation are needed before it can support comparisons across settings or evaluation of improvements in dialysis access care.

S.; Campbell, J.; Cederroth, C. R.; De Ridder, D.; Husain, F. T.; Langguth, B.; Neff, P.; Schlee, W.; Vanneste, S.
after.abstract: Identifying reliable neural biomarkers of chronic tinnitus remains challenging because ageing and hearing loss independently influence auditory cortical activity. Here, we investigated auditory expectation processing in 440 adults with (n = 226) and without (n = 214) chronic tinnitus using electroencephalography during a local-global auditory paradigm across six centres. Although several electrophysiological group differences emerged in unadjusted analyses, most were substantially attenuated after adjustment for demographic and audiological factors. Two clusters remained significant within the unexpected-omission-versus-sound contrast (44 to 100 ms and 356 to 476 ms), but neither survived correction across eight contrasts. Direct comparisons between expected and unexpected omissions revealed no significant group differences. Exploratory classification using selected EEG features achieved a cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.624, increasing to 0.689 when combined with demographic and audiological predictors. However, this improvement was not reproduced in held-out validation, and EEG features showed limited predictive value for tinnitus burden or loudness. These findings highlight a fundamental distinction between electrophysiological group differences and clinically informative individual-level biomarkers, underscoring the importance of controlling for confounding factors and establishing independent predictive validity in tinnitus research.

after.abstract: Background Natalizumab, an 4-integrin monoclonal antibody, a highly effective relapsing multiple sclerosis (MS) therapy, carries a small but clinically important risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Previous studies have suggested that alternative dosing paradigms can reduce PML risk while maintaining therapeutic efficacy. Objectives Clarify how immune cell dynamics changes with the alternative dosing. Methods We investigated alternative dosing paradigms by profiling cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) immune cell dynamics across: (1) standard interval dosing (SID, every 4 weeks), (2) extended interval dosing (EID, every 6 or 8 weeks), and (3) annual 12-week gap (aGAP). Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we analyzed 46 CSF samples from participants across dosing regimens, untreated MS controls, and one non-natalizumab-related PML case. Results Compared with controls, natalizumab reduced proportions of Treg, memory T cells, B cells, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, while increasing tissue-resident memory T and microglia-like myeloid cells. EID and aGAP were associated with higher proportions of peripheral immune populations, including CD4+ T cells with interferon response signatures (CD4+IFN+), potentially enhancing antiviral immunity. The PML case exhibited elevated CD8+ central memory T and CD56bright NK cells proportions in the CSF, suggesting their role in viral control. Conclusions These findings support that EID and aGAP allow immune reconstitution.

after.authors: Xue, Y.; Hao, Y.; Shi, C.; Sun, X.; Li, K.; Li, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Gynecology, Anyang Cancer Hospital, Anyang, Henan Province, China
after.abstract: Objective: This study examined whether adding sintilimab to standard treatment improves early tumor response and survival in locally advanced cervical cancer. We also determined how peripheral CD8+ T-cell counts and the tumor marker CA125 change from baseline to treatment completion, and whether these measures predict the benefit of combination therapy. Method: We enrolled 126 patients with locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC; FIGO 2018 stage IB3-IVA) treated at our institution between January 2023 and January 2025 in this single-center retrospective cohort. Sixty-six received standard concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT), and 60 received CCRT plus sintilimab (200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks throughout the treatment course). Peripheral blood samples were obtained at baseline and at treatment completion to quantify CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell proportions and serum CA125 levels. Short-term response was assessed by RECIST version 1.1. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method and compared between groups with the log-rank test. Independent prognostic factors were identified using Cox proportional hazards regression, and likelihood ratio tests examined interactions between immune markers and treatment assignment. Results: The objective response rate (ORR) was 81.67% with CCRT plus sintilimab versus 65.15% with CCRT alone (P = 0.045). Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 18.6 months in the combination group and 10.0 months in the CCRT group (log-rank P < 0.001). Median overall survival (OS) was not reached in the combination group but was 27.3 months in the CCRT group (log-rank P = 0.0027). After adjustment for age and BMI, combination therapy remained an independent favorable prognostic factor for both PFS (HR = 0.443, 95% CI: 0.290-0.678, P < 0.001) and OS (HR = 0.410, 95% CI: 0.230-0.731, P = 0.002). Stratification by the median post-treatment peripheral CD8+ T-cell proportion (24.48%) gave a median PFS of 19.9 months in the high-CD8+ group versus 12.4 months in the low-CD8+ group (HR = 0.63, 95% CI: 0.42-0.94, P = 0.022). CD8+ T-cell stratification showed a significant interaction with treatment assignment for OS (P = 0.012). Using the median post-treatment CA125 level (31.25 IU/mL), median PFS was 11.9 months in the high-CA125 group versus 19.4 months in the low-CA125 group (HR = 1.89, 95% CI: 1.26-2.83, P = 0.0017); unlike CD8+ stratification, however, CA125 showed no significant interaction with treatment for either PFS (P = 0.959) or OS (P = 0.569). Conclusion: In LACC, concurrent chemoradiotherapy combined with sintilimab improves objective response and is associated with longer PFS and OS. Patients with a higher post-treatment CD8+ T-cell proportion derive greater benefit from combination therapy, supporting its use as a stratification indicator of efficacy. CA125 mainly reflects tumor burden and overall prognosis rather than treatment benefit and is therefore unsuitable for selecting patients for immunotherapy.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Population Health Sciences, Geisinger, Danville, PA, USA
after.abstract: Background: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Analyzing the sequence and timing of clinical events before treatment can reveal barriers to early non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) diagnosis and care. Methods: We established a retrospective cohort of 3541 adult patients diagnosed between 2012 and 2022, and received all or part of their initial treatment within our health system. Sequences of pre-treatment clinical events including imaging, primary care provider (PCP) and lung specialist visits, Emergency Department (ED) presentation, diagnosis, and treatment type were encoded using 1-gram and 2-gram representations. K-means clustering, guided by the Gap Statistic method, determined the optimal pathway groups. Results: Four distinct care pathways were identified: (1) Low-Dose Computed Tomography (LDCT) Screening (n=215), with high LDCT use (98.6%) and early-stage diagnoses (67.0%), yielding the highest 5-year survival rate (72.1%). (2) Moderate Early-Stage Detection (MESD) (n=1236) showed the second-highest rate of early-stage diagnoses (53.2%) with minimal LDCT uptake (0.3%) and the lowest rate of primary care engagement (15.2%). (3) High Comorbidity Burden (HCB) (n=1200), with the highest Charlson index (5), low early-stage diagnosis (36.5%), and low LDCT referral rates (3%). (4) ED Presentation (EDP) (n=890), with frequent ED visits prior to diagnosis (65.5%), low LDCT referral (1.2%), and the lowest rate of early-stage detection (19.8%). Conclusion: Distinct routes revealed unmet needs, including limited LDCT screening, low primary care engagement in MESD, and barriers to early medical attention in the EDP group. Targeted interventions may enable early detection and improve survival.

after.authors: Chen, D. Z.; Ma, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health
after.abstract: Sex differences in minor allele frequency (sdMAF) are widely used as a quality control (QC) metric for variants in the non-pseudoautosomal region (NPR) of the X chromosome. However, conventional sdMAF tests assess marginal allele-frequency differences and generally do not account for imbalances in measured covariates, such as genetic ancestry. We develop a general regression-based framework for covariate-adjusted subgroup allele-frequency inference. Using the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem, we derive adjusted subgroup mean estimators and their joint sampling covariance under a groupwise residual-variance structure, enabling both targeted one-degree-of-freedom tests and joint tests of multiple subgroup contrasts. For X-NPR sdMAF analysis, we consider a parsimonious groupwise variance estimator motivated by the distinct genotype distributions of hemizygous males and diploid females, alongside the conventional homoskedastic and heteroskedasticity-robust HC1 estimators. Simulation studies evaluate Type I error control, robustness to Hardy-Weinberg disequilibrium, and statistical power. The homoskedastic variance estimator exhibited Type I error distortion under imbalanced sex ratios, whereas HC1 and the groupwise estimator demonstrated broadly comparable Type I error control and power across the simulated scenarios. In an application to 1000 Genomes Project data, adjusted and unadjusted sdMAF estimates were highly correlated, although covariate adjustment altered effect estimates and statistical significance for individual variants. The framework also supports a theoretical extension to sex-prevalence-adjusted allelic contrasts, with groupwise variance estimation providing a parsimonious alternative to HC1 for X-NPR sdMAF analysis.

At week 4, total AAT concentrations were 15.4 M in the patient who received 35 mg and a mean of 19.0 M in the 45-mg cohort, with increases sustained for up to 11 months. after.abstract: Glycosylation is a prevalent post-translational modification in the human brain, but its genetic regulation remains poorly defined. We profiled N-linked glycosylation in 316 human prefrontal cortices and generated the first glycoproteome-wide map of glycosylation quantitative trait loci (glycoQTLs). GlycoQTLs were enriched in regulatory regions and partly independent of protein abundance. High-mannose glycopeptiforms were preferentially affected, suggesting genetic influence on early glycan processing in the endoplasmic reticulum. Integration with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) GWAS summary statistics identified disease-associated glycoQTLs, including those at TMEM106B and ACE. At TMEM106B, the ADRD risk allele altered the glycan composition at N183 within the fibril-forming C-terminal fragment of the protein, whereas at ACE, individual glycopeptiforms showed divergent genetic effects. Targeted trans-glycoQTL analysis further identified long-range regulation, including a hotspot at the fucosidase FUCA2. These findings establish glycoQTL mapping as a complementary functional-genomics layer that reveals disease-associated molecular effects beyond conventional protein-level analyses.

after.title: Preprint: Human genetic support improves the odds of drug success but poorly predicts it
after.authors: Kohleick, L.; Pietzner, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Berlin Institute of Health (BIH) at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin
after.abstract: Nine in ten drug programmes that enter clinical trials fail, mostly for lack of efficacy1,2. Drug targets supported by human genetic evidence are about twice as likely to reach approval3-5, which now guides target selection. Yet most of it emerged only after the drugs had been developed, the methods linking genetic variants to genes were trained in part on known drug targets6, and recent trials of genetically supported targets have both lowered a disease marker7 and failed to reduce clinical events8,9. Here we tested how far genetic support can guide drug development across almost 17,000 target-disease pairs. Its association with clinical success held when genes were assigned without knowledge of drugs, within diseases and for evidence available years before a trial. It was strongest where the evidence pointed directly to the causal gene, larger for diseases judged on a measurable trait, and absent for drugs that use their target only to reach cells, such as antibody-drug conjugates. Genetic support, however, contributed little to distinguishing successful from failed programmes. Human genetic evidence is therefore a reliable but modest guide to where to invest, not a predictor of which programme will succeed.

after.title: Preprint: A Cost Analysis of 10-Year Versus 20-Year Glass Slide Retention in the Era of Whole Slide Imaging
after.authors: Cecchini, M. J.; Tremblay-LeMay, R.; Beyer, D.; Yousef, G. M.
after.abstract: Background. The Canadian Association of Pathologists recommends keeping glass slides for 20 years, a recommendation made before digital pathology; United States regulation requires 10 years and United Kingdom guidance permits 8 years when the block is kept. Glass is inexpensive to store, whereas digital whole slide images (WSI) incur recurring storage charges, and how often old material is requested has rarely been measured. Methods. A deterministic cost model (2026 Canadian dollars) compared 10- and 20-year rules in illustrative laboratories accessioning 100,000, 500,000, and 750,000 slides/year under three strategies: glass only, glass plus WSI of every slide, and glass plus a hypothetical selective WSI archive. Requests for discarded glass were met by recuts. Because no published data describe second-decade requests, their share was set at an illustrative 0.5%, varied from 0% to 2%, and break-even thresholds were calculated. Off-site glass storage was a secondary analysis. Results. For glass only, the 20-year rule cost less than the 10-year rule only if more than 0.32% of slides were requested at ages 10 to 19 years (or, at 0.5%, if recuts cost more than CAD 14.54 per slide); at 0.5% it was 6.6% to 6.9% cheaper, and at 0.01% 14.6% to 14.9% more expensive. With WSI of every slide, 20-year retention increased annual costs by 35.3% to 36.8% (CAD 153,210/year, academic laboratory). Keeping glass 20 years and WSI 10 years removed this increase. Selective WSI was cheapest only under favourable selection assumptions. Off-site glass storage after the first year added 43% to 62%. Conclusions. Whether a 20-year glass rule costs more than a 10-year rule depends on how often old glass is requested, which is largely unknown; applied to digital images, a 20-year rule added substantial cost unless more than about 1.7% of slides were requested in their second decade. Flexibility in storage rules can allow laboratories to optimize storage for cost and access to diagnostic material.

after.authors: Ilada, A. G.; Abulude, I. J.; Singh, S.; Osagie, E.; Akhigbe, P.; Kumar, A.; Obuekwe, O.; Bocarsly, P.; Richards, V. P.; Coker, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Pennsylvania - School of Dental Medicine
after.abstract: Background: Despite antiretroviral therapy (ART), children living with HIV (HI) experience a disproportionate burden of oral diseases, including dental caries. It remains unclear whether this increased susceptibility is associated with altered local expression of inflammatory cytokines, and whether systemic inflammatory profiles reflect corresponding immune signals in saliva. Methods: We analyzed 10 plasma and 7 salivary cytokines in matched plasma and unstimulated saliva samples from 467 Nigerian children aged 4-11 years: HI (n = 144), HEU (n = 161), and HUU (n = 162). Correlation analyses assessed plasma-saliva concordance, PERMANOVA evaluated overall cytokine profiles, multivariable linear regression examined individual cytokines, and network density analysis quantified connectivity. Results: Cytokines correlated more strongly within than between compartments. HIV exposure and infection status were associated with overall cytokine profiles in plasma (R^2 = 0.008, p = 0.038) and saliva (R^2 = 0.017, p < 0.001), and pairwise differences between comparison groups were significant only in saliva. HI children had higher plasma IL-5 and MCP-1 and higher salivary IL-6 and MCP-1 than HEU and HUU children. Higher CD4 T-cell count was associated with lower plasma IL-6 and MCP-1 and lower salivary IL-6. Caries status was not associated with overall cytokine profiles, but salivary IL-4 was higher in caries-free children. Conclusions: Plasma and salivary cytokines capture largely distinct immune signals in children affected by HIV, and saliva does not appear to serve as a surrogate for plasma with respect to cytokine expression. We did observe that HIV infection and immune status, not dental caries, were the main correlates of cytokine variation in plasma and saliva compartments.

after.title: Preprint: Outcomes of tracing antiretroviral therapy clients after missed clinic visits in South Africa: A retrospective cohort analysis
after.authors: Mutanda, N.; Ntjikelane, V.; Kachingwe, E.; Sande, L.; Maskew, M.; Benade, M.; Mangane, M.; Malala, L.; Marri, A.; Rosen, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA
after.abstract: Background In South Africa, interruption of antiretroviral therapy (ART) (missing a clinic visit or medication refill) for more than 28 days is very common, with an estimated 60% of clients interrupting at least once during their first year after initiation. Healthcare worker tracing of those who miss visits or medication refills, either through phone calls, text messages, or home visits (physical tracing), is a globally recommended, near-universal component of national HIV programs, but little is known about its effectiveness in returning clients to care. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of clients eligible for tracing under the South African national guidelines (7 or more days late for a scheduled visit) at 15 public-sector ART clinics between January 2024 and August 2025. Tracing records were abstracted from facility paper registers and linked to electronic medical records to determine outcomes. We report tracing contact status (reached directly, reached indirectly through family member or friend, not reached, unknown) and final outcomes (return to care, self-return, no return, transfer/death, misidentification), separately for telephone and physical tracing, including time to return to care using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results Tracing was attempted for 5,161 clients by telephone and 3,902 by physical visit. Roughly half of clients could be reached by tracers, either directly (43% telephone, 47% physical) or indirectly (7% telephone, 7% physical). Among those reached directly, 62-65% returned to care after contact. Among those who could not be reached, most nonetheless self-returned to care without any tracing contact (73% telephone, 65% physical), though more slowly than those who were reached. By day 90, two thirds of those reached directly by phone (68%) or physically (70%) had returned to care, compared to 60% and 53% of those not reached. Roughly 15% of tracing attempts targeted clients who had already returned to care, transferred, died, or had never actually interrupted care, reflecting data-quality challenges in the tracing and medical record systems. Conclusions Tracing HIV treatment clients who have missed clinic visits or medication pickups in South Africa appears to accelerate return to care but has an unclear effect on the overall proportion of those who return. Current data systems hamper efficient tracing efforts. Digitizing paper tracing registers, more targeted tracing that focuses limited resources on clients who genuinely require outreach, and interventions that promote client-initiated updates and two-way communication could allow better allocation of tracing resources to those truly in need.

after.authors: Owuor, D. C.; Cheruiyot, C. K.; Onyango, M.; Ombija, S. O.; Barmasai, S.; Nzunza, R.; Hassan, J.; Ali, S.; Chepkurui, A.; Ndunge, A.; Komen, E.; Mwangi, B.; Oswago, L. O.; Kipchirchir, C.; Gathenji, C.; Kipterer, J.; Mwanza, M. N.; Touray, K.; Ali, A.; Mdodo, R.; Khamadi, S. A.; Borus, P.
after.abstract: The poliovirus eradication campaign by the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) has resulted in the eradication of wild poliovirus (WPV) serotypes two (WPV2) and three (WPV3) and limited transmission of serotype one (WPV1) in two countries. However, increased emergence of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) outbreaks and continued circulation of WPV1 poses a continuous threat of international spread. Recently, cVDPV serotype 2 (cVDPV2) isolates from environmental samples in five World Health Organization (WHO) European Region (EURO) countries were genetically linked to cVDPV2 originating in Nigeria. We utilized phylogeographic methods to infer the origins and geographic spread cVDPV2 poliovirus in WHO African Region (AFRO) Horn of Africa using 234 full-length VP1 gene sequences from three WHO AFRO and one WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMRO) countries collected through clinical and environmental surveillance between 2017 and 2025. cVDPV2 outbreak strains from different countries in the Horn of Africa spanned the overall SOM-BAN-1 phylogeny, reflecting multiple introductions into the region, with strains harboring unique nucleotide mutations and amino acid substitutions. Phylogeographic analyses revealed SOM-BAN-1 origins from Somalia, with subsequent spread to other Horn of African countries and subsequent seeding of cVDPV2 outbreaks from other countries in the region, but with phylogenetic predominance of Somalia. The cVDPV2 transmission dynamics in the region were characterized by circulation of multiple chains of transmission in multiple countries, with poliovirus spread characterized by localized evolution and regionally linked chains of transmission. Stronger evidence for SOM-BAN-1 origins from Somalia was observed, with multiple chains of transmission observed in multiple sub-national locations, supporting the important role played by the country in the predominance and persistence of cVDPV2 in Horn of Africa region. The spread of cVDPV2 outside the country of first detection, with further international spread, reveals gaps in the effectiveness and timeliness of outbreak responses. Therefore, regular updates of poliovirus surveillance sequence data using phylogeographic tools may provide insights into changes in poliovirus epidemiology, which can in turn guide the implementation of timely outbreak response and more strategic and effective vaccination campaigns. The analyses may be particularly relevant to understand the evolutionary and transmission dynamics of ongoing cVDPV outbreaks in AFRO, halting ongoing transmissions in AFRO and recent spread to other regions, achieving the GPEIs efforts of a poliovirus-free world.

after.abstract: Gait variability and physical fitness may provide accessible indicators of brain health in aging, yet their associations with resting-state dynamic functional connectivity remain unclear. We examined associations of gait variability and physical fitness with local and distant temporal consistency of resting-state dynamic functional connectivity in 86 cognitively normal older adults from the AGUEDA trial. Gait variability was assessed using coefficients of variation for stride length, gait velocity, step time, and step length, while physical fitness included muscular strength and cardiorespiratory fitness. Dynamic functional connectivity was estimated using voxel-wise stepwise connectivity analyses. Analyses targeting regions related to Alzheimers disease risk and exploratory whole-brain analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and education. Greater gait variability was associated with local, but not distant, temporal consistency of dynamic functional connectivity. Greater stride length, gait velocity, and step length variability were associated with higher local temporal consistency in the left inferior frontal gyrus ({beta} = 0.28 to 0.33; false discovery rate-corrected P = 0.024 to 0.047) and lower temporal consistency in the right insula ({beta} = -0.47 to -0.31; false discovery rate-corrected P = 0.001 to 0.028). Whole-brain analyses revealed lower local temporal consistency in the left parahippocampal gyrus with greater stride length variability ({beta} = -0.43; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.002) and in the left calcarine cortex with greater gait velocity variability ({beta} = -0.45; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.001). No statistically significant associations were observed for physical fitness. These findings suggest that gait variability may reflect aspects of local dynamic functional brain organization in cognitively normal older adults.

after.authors: Zeggane, S.; Mslmane, A.; Fleuriet, J.; Heming, N.; Bacq-Daian, D.; Olaso, R.; Deleuze, J.-F.; Annane, D.; Garchon, H.-J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Paris-Saclay University, UVSQ, INSERM U1173, Infection and Inflammation Laboratory, Montigny-le-Bretonneux, France
after.abstract: Sepsis is a highly prevalent and life-threatening syndrome resulting from an exaggerated inflammatory response to an infection. Its etiology is multifactorial and involves both environmental and genetic factors that are presently poorly understood. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) on sepsis patients survival at 90-day following admission in the ICU. We extracted genotypes of single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) from whole-genome sequencing data of 1030 patients from three cohorts, including APROCCHSS, RECORDS-Observational and TRIAL. We used a proportional hazard Cox model adjusted for age, the first two genetic principal components and the cohort. We identified 7 significant SNVs that reached genome-wide significance (P<5 x 10-8). One of them, rs1474684, maps to the last intron of the phospholipase C Beta 1 (PLCB1) gene and likely is causative, following fine-mapping. Two other SNVs map to IMPDH1P7 gene for rs146038228 and CALCRL-AS1 for rs4667156. Both genes lie in a 400 kb region showing extended linkage disequilibrium that prevented resolution of the causative variant. The other four variants were low frequency SNVs mapping to non-coding or intergenic regions near ENSG00000288587 (rs11754929), ENSG00000248172 (rs74570843), ISG20 (rs139793868), and RNU6-144P (rs78812419). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis, a sensitive nonparametric method to rank pathways associated with variants and genes, consistently highlighted terms associated with the central nervous system, synapse physiology and cardio-endocrine regulation. Altogether, our findings shed new light on genetic factors and pathways associated with survival in sepsis patients. However, further investigation in an independent cohort will be necessary for validation of the associations.

after.authors: Leistle, H.; Dadar, M.; morrison, C.
after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Estrogen is thought to be neuroprotective; however, estrogen drops during menopause. Hormone-replacement therapy (HRT) could prevent cognitive decline in females by replacing endogenous estrogen. However, research has generated contradictory findings on whether HRT benefits cognition in females. The current study explores the influence of estrogen-only HRT and estrogen-progestin HRT on cognitive performance in females over time. METHODS: Longitudinal data from 22,706 female participants aged 55+ (n = 1336 estrogen-only HRT, n = 144 estrogen-progestin HRT, n = 21,226 no HRT) was included from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center. Linear mixed-effect models examined the relationships between HRT conditions and cognitive functioning over time. RESULTS: Both types of HRT were associated with slower decline in cognition, with combination HRT predicting better cognitive outcomes than estrogen-only HRT. DISCUSSION: The findings suggest that HRT may offer protective effects for cognition over time, especially estrogen-progestin HRT, contrary to some previous research; however, more research is needed.

after.authors: Irfan, A.; Jadoon, K. K.; Hanif, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Ghulam Ishaq Khan Institute of Engineering Sciences and Technology, Topi, Pakistan
after.abstract: Automated twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has historically relied on discriminative classifiers limited to closed-set diagnostic labels, signal reconstruction, or saliency heatmaps. While categorizing predefined arrhythmias well, these static classifiers cannot generate narrative clinical reports, incorporate patient history, or support interactive clinical question-answering (Q&A). We present LifeLine.ai, an end-toend multimodal Vision-ECG-Language framework for automated cardiac diagnosis and clinical reporting. After early attempts at waveform peak-tracking and coordinate mapping failed against complex morphological variations, we leveraged large-scale PhysioNet repositories (MIMIC-IV and PTB-XL). Because hardware limits precluded training on over 800,000 raw records, we curated a balanced subset to estimate performance, converting one-dimensional signals into 3x4 twelve-lead grids with continuous Lead II rhythm strips at the bottom. Our pipeline integrates YOLOv11s localization, a LoRAadapted Google SigLIP encoder, a trainable Multi-Layer Perceptron projector, and a 4-bit quantized MedGemma-4B model, complemented by a separate Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) pipeline built on collected user feedback and a multi-LLM consensus engine. On this compact subset, SigLIP outperformed Swin Transformer encodings (~0.21 vs. ~0.25 validation loss), achieving 71.0% open-vocabulary precision and a 75.0% contextual F1 score across a cloud deployment spanning Vercel, mobile apps, Amazon EC2, Firebase, Hugging Face, Modal GPUs, and lifelinecg-sdk. Our code is available at https://github.com/Asad939asad/ LifeLine.ai-.

after.authors: Lopez Pineda, A.; Tripp, J.; Santana-Quinteros, D.; Flores-Garrido, M.; Garcia-Velazquez, L. M.; Figueroa-Mora, K. M.; Gomez-Garcia, A.; Alvarez-Aguilar, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Universidad Michoacana de San Nicolas de Hidalgo
after.abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) from primary care are scarce in low- and middle-income countries, and few have been made available to researchers in Latin America. We present DiabetIA, a longitudinal dataset derived from the primary care records of the Mexican Institute of Social Security (IMSS). The first release comprises 136,674 adults followed in six IMSS family medicine units in the state of Michoacan between 2005 and 2020, with more than 3.2 million visits summarized in 414,770 two-year windows with at least one visit. Each window includes demographics, ICD-10 diagnoses, anthropometry, vital signs, laboratory results and prescriptions, and type 2 diabetes diagnoses in the following year as prediction targets. At baseline, 24.4% of the patients had type 2 diabetes, 37.1% hypertension and 32.3% obesity. Technical validation assessed completeness, plausibility, consistency, temporal coverage and agreement with a state health survey. DiabetIA is freely available for download to support research on chronic disease trajectories and prediction in an underrepresented population.

after.title: Preprint: Retention in care and viral suppression among people on HIV treatment receiving 6- versus 12-month prescriptions in South Africa: a cohort study using routinely collected electronic health data
after.authors: Mokgethi, N. O.; Huber, A. N.; Shumba, K.; Munsamy, M.; Ramdas, N.; Jamieson, l.; Rosen, S.; Pillay, M.; Pascoe, S.; Manganye, M.; Malala, L.; Fox, M. P.; Miot, J.; Mokhele, I.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Health Economics and Epidemiology Research Office, School of clinical medicine, University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, South Africa
after.abstract: Introduction During the COVID-19 pandemic, ART prescription lengths in South Africa were temporarily extended from six months to twelve months for stable clients, reducing required clinic visits from two to one per year. We compared retention and viral suppression outcomes between clients receiving 6-month and 12-month prescriptions within South Africa's Centralised Chronic Medicines Dispensing and Distribution (CCMDD) programme, which serves over 3.2 million people living with HIV through medication collection at facility-based or community-based pickup points. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study in seven South African provinces using routinely collected electronic health data. We included adults ([≥]18) with a 6-month or 12-month ART prescription issued between June and November 2020. Participants were followed for 24 months. Retention was defined as [≥]1 medication collection visit during months 13-24 of follow-up and viral suppression as a viral load <50 copies/ml at the first test conducted in that window. We estimated unadjusted retention and suppression rates and then used a modified Poisson regression model with a log link and robust standard errors to compare non-retention and viral non-suppression between groups, accounting for district-level clustering and adjusting for age, sex, time on ART, model of care, and ART regimen. Results: Among 428,926 clients, 196,531 (46%) received 6-month prescriptions and 232,395 (54%) received 12-month prescriptions. During the outcome assessment period (months 13 to 24), clients in the 6-month group attended a median of 2 clinical prescribing visits and clients in the 12-month group attended a median of 1 clinical prescribing visit. Unadjusted retention was 91.4% in the 6-month group and 91.6% in the 12-month group; viral suppression was 79.3% in the 6-month group and 80.9% in the 12-month group. After adjustment, using the 6-month prescription group as the reference, adjusted risk ratios were 0.98 (0.91-1.05) for non-retention and 0.93 (0.82-1.06) for viral non-suppression. Conclusion: Twelve-month prescriptions maintained retention in care and viral suppression rates equal to 6-month prescriptions while halving required annual clinic visits per client. These findings support further evaluation of reduced-frequency prescribing within differentiated HIV service delivery programmes for stable clients and contribute to the evidence base to guide recommendations on reduced clinical prescribing visits.
