after.authors: Grimaud, O.; Martin, S.; Ricard-Hibon, A.; Pottecher, J.; Philippe, J.-M.; Leray, E.; Bayat, S.; Braun, F.; Carli, P.; Tattevin, P.; Noizet, M.; Sanchez, M.-A.; Dolz, M.; Vuagnat, A.; Maury, E.; Chauliac, N.; Coignard, H.; Prieto, N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Univ Rennes, EHESP, CNRS, ARENES - UMR 6051, Rennes
after.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
after.abstract: Objectives Even taking into account the selection of healthier patients, it has been shown that the mass transfers of patients between intensive care units (ICUs) outside their own region during the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in France was associated with lower mortality but a higher rate of psychiatric disorders in the ICU. In other countries, the survival benefit of such transfers had faded after around 60 days. Our aim was to determine the long-term outcomes (up to one year) associated with these mass transfers in France. Design TRANSCOV retrospective cohort study enriched by data linkage with hospital admissions, outpatient consultations, prescriptions and deaths database. Setting Multi-centre study involving 39 origin ICUs from the East and Paris regions (France) and 57 destination ICUs located in regions then unaffected by the pandemic. Participants Patients with severe COVID-19 (n = 1,113) admitted to ICUs in the Eastern and Paris regions between 4 March 2020 and 10 April 2020. Exposure Being transferred from versus remaining in overburdened ICUs. Outcome measures The main outcome was death occurring during the year following admission in ICU. Secondary outcomes related to the mental health of participants during follow-up including hospital admission with a psychiatric disorder as the main or associated diagnosis, outpatient psychiatric consultation and psychotropic drugs prescription. Results At initial admission, patients in the transfer (n=319) and the control (n=794) groups were similar in age (64 years), sex (74% male), number of comorbidities and severity. However, transferred patients were lighter (- 8kg, p<0.001). Respectively 44 and 309 deaths were recorded in the transfer and control groups, the vast majority of which occurring while in ICU. At the end of follow-up, the adjusted incidence rate ratio associated with transfer was 0.18 (95% CI:0.13-0.24) thus suggesting a five-fold lower mortality risk. Transferred patients experienced twice as many psychiatric disorders during initial ICU stay (39.2% versus 18.3%, p<0.001) and these disorders were more often reported as associated (never as main) diagnosis of subsequent hospitalizations (28.8% versus 22%, p=0.04). However, both groups had similar rates of outpatient psychiatric consultations and prescriptions of psychotropic drugs during follow-up. Conclusions Mass extra-regional inter ICU transfers organised in France in spring 2020 were associated with both short- and long-term survival benefit. Mass-transfer to alleviate overcrowding should be considered an appropriate response to future sudden and localised increase in the demand for intensive care.

IntroductionStroma areactive invasion front areas (SARIFA) are a histopathological phenomenon at the tumour invasion front characterised by direct tumour-adipocyte contact (TAC). It can be detected on histological Haematoxylin-Eosin (H&E) stained tumour slides. TAC/SARIFA has emerged as a strong negative prognostic factor in several tumour entities. In this monocentric retrospective study, we aim to elucidate the impact of TAC/SARIFA in oropharyngeal cancer.

Materials and methods78 cases of pT3 - pT4 oropharyngeal squamous cell cancer from 2005 to 2023 and their corresponding lymph nodes were analysed for the occurrence of TAC/SARIFA. Besides, we compared overall survival rates, recurrence-free survival (RFS) and association with biological and pathological tumour characteristics.

ResultsIn total, overall survival was significantly reduced in TAC/SARIFA-positive tumours (p=0.014). Moreover, TAC/SARIFA-positive primary tumours are associated with TAC/SARIFA-positive lymph nodes (p<0.001) and extranodal extension (ENE) (p=0.032). Finally, RFS in TAC/SARIFA-positive tumours was reduced, but not significantly (p=0.072). No significant difference was found between p16-positive and p16-negative tumours and prevalence of TAC/SARIFA.

ConclusionTAC/SARIFA is a possible prognostically relevant risk factor in oropharyngeal cancer. When detected in the primary tumour or lymph nodes, it is associated with reduced overall survival rates and tendency towards shorter RFS. TAC/SARIFA-positive lymph nodes almost always show ENE.

after.abstract:
BackgroundAchromobacter are a genus of difficult-to-treat, frequently multi-drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria that can cause severe infections in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Bacteriophages are an understudied yet promising therapy for these and other antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, data are largely limited to case reports or series, and clinical trials among pwCF to date have not evaluated Achromobacter.

MethodsThis is an investigator-initiated, open-label, randomized phase 1 pilot trial to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and biological effects of AchromoPhage, a cocktail of four genetically distinct, obligately lytic Achromobacter-targeting phages (phiACH01, phiACH04, phiACH06, phiACH07) with broad activity against Achromobacter species, in 12 adult participants with CF and pulmonary Achromobacter infection. Twelve participants will be randomized into three groups to receive a total of three, increasing, weekly doses of the AchromoPhage cocktail via one of three routes: 1) intravenous, 2) via inhalation, or 3) or intravenously and inhaled. Participation in the trial will span approximately 7 weeks, which will consist of outpatient phage dose administrations, safety and symptom monitoring, and longitudinal collection of biospecimens for protocol-specified and exploratory analyses through Day 42. The primary safety endpoint is the occurrence of treatment-related Grade 4 or greater adverse events. Secondary endpoints include longitudinal changes in FEV1 by spirometry, longitudinal changes in health-related quality of life, pharmacokinetics of each of the four phages in blood and the respiratory tract, and emergence of a phage neutralizing antibody response in serum.

DiscussionWhile existing case anecdotes and observational studies suggest that phages are safe and may have a role in treating human infections, there is a paucity of clinical trials studying the adverse effect profile and basic pharmacological parameters of phages. This trial will study the safety and explore the pharmacokinetic and other properties of a four-phage cocktail in patients with CF and chronic Achromobacter lung infection.

Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT0727590. Registered on 12/10/2025

after.title: Preprint: Association between Social Media Exposure and Self-Medication Practices: Public Health Implications in Punjab, Pakistan
after.authors: Ashraf, A.; Saddique, M. A. B.; Sajid, M. S.; Anjum, S.; Rizwan, F.; Qasim, M. Z.
after.abstract:
BackgroundSocial media has become an important source of health information, including information about medicines. Exposure to medicine-related content may affect decisions to use medicines without professional consultation.

ObjectiveTo describe self-medication practices and social-media exposure among adults in Punjab, Pakistan, and explore associations between self-medication frequency and demographic, social-media-use, and attitudinal factors. Methods: A cross-sectional analytical survey was conducted among adults aged 18-60 years in Punjab between March and May 2026. The final analytic sample comprised 280 participants. A bilingual (Urdu/English) questionnaire assessed demographics, social-media use and health-content exposure, self-medication in the preceding six months, medicine categories, and attitudes. The questionnaire was reviewed by two clinical experts and piloted among 30 participants. Descriptive analyses, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression were reported using IBM SPSS Statistics; significance was set at =.05.

ResultsSelf-medication frequency was reported as Rarely by 117 participants (41.8%), Frequently by 130 (46.4%), and More Often by 33 (11.8%). Fever medicines were reported by 179 participants (63.9%) and gastrointestinal medicines by 96 (34.3%); multiple-response medicine categories were not mutually exclusive. Instagram was the most frequently selected social-media platform. Advertisement recall differed across self-medication frequency groups ({chi}2(22)=35.28, p=.036). Belief that medicines shown in advertisements/posts were safe was associated with self-medication frequency ({chi}2(4)=14.26, p=.007), while perceived risk was not ({chi}2(4)=1.587, p=.811). The multinomial models overall test was not statistically significant ({chi}2(40)=54.07, p=.068; Nagelkerke R2=.205). Likelihood-ratio tests identified associations for daily social-media-use duration ({chi}2(2)=13.085, p=.001), age group ({chi}2(6)=14.930, p=.021), and perceived advertisement safety ({chi}2(4)=10.899, p=.028).

ConclusionSelf-medication was commonly reported in this sample. Some social-media-use and advertising-attitude variables were associated with self-medication frequency, but the overall regression model was not statistically significant and the cross-sectional design cannot establish causality. Findings should be interpreted cautiously given the sample composition and reported data limitations.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Bladder scanning in children: accuracy of volume estimation and detection of urinary retention

after.title: Preprint: Bladder scanning in children: accuracy of volume estimation and detection of urinary retention
after.authors: de Jong, A. C.; Arguedas Flores, O. E.; van Woensel, J. B. M.; Keunen, K.; Eijken, G. V.; de Kraker, T. M.; Maaskant, J. M.
after.abstract:
ObjectivesAccurate bladder volume assessment supports catheterization decisions in children, but evidence for the accuracy of automated bladder scanners is limited. In a large pediatric cohort, we assessed agreement between bladder scanner-estimated and catheterized volumes, and diagnostic accuracy for detecting urinary retention and elevated post-void residual (PVR).

Study designThis prospective cross-sectional study was conducted at a tertiary pediatric hospital. Children aged 0-12 years underwent bladder scanning (CUBEScan BioCon-900S) prior to clinically indicated catheterization or cystoscopy. Agreement was assessed using correlation and Bland-Altman analyses. Urinary retention (catheterized volume exceeding expected bladder capacity) and elevated PVR ([≥]4 years) were defined using age-specific thresholds.

ResultsIn 189 paired measurements from 181 children (median age 2.4 years), correlation was strong ({rho}=0.86). Despite a small mean difference (2 mL), 95% limits of agreement were wide (-91 to 95 mL), and only 38% of measurements were within {+/-}20% of catheterized volume. Agreement was moderate in children 2-12 years, and lowest in children <2 years and at volumes <100 mL. Overall specificity for urinary retention was 0.88, but sensitivity only 0.75, reflecting underestimation of elevated volumes, with an area under the curve of 0.75 overall versus 0.91 [≥]2 years. For elevated PVR, overall sensitivity was 0.98, but specificity 0.63.

ConclusionsBladder scanner-estimated volumes correlated well with catheterized volumes but showed limited agreement, particularly in children <2 years. This device is therefore not recommended in this age group. In older children, it may serve as an adjunct to clinical assessment of urinary retention.

after.authors: Lazari, A.; Broulidakis, J.; Gillis, G.; Bhalerao, G.; Halls, D.; Wickham, F.; Tendler, B. C.; Sotiropoulos, S. N.; Griffanti, L.; Husain, M.; Mars, R. B.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Oxford Centre for Integrative Neuroimaging (OxCIN), FMRIB, Nuffield Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Oxford
after.abstract:
BackgroundNeurodegenerative disorders are common in ageing populations, and arise from several distinct pathophysiological causes. Yet, they also share many symptoms, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric ones. It is unclear to what extent the impact of neurodegeneration on brain systems is unique or shared across disorders, and whether shared symptoms are driven by degeneration of the same brain systems.

MethodsWe collected data from n=251 participants with Alzheimers Disease, Parkinsons Disease, Small Vessel Disease, and age-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessment and were scanned using the UK-Biobank MRI protocol capturing features including brain volume, white matter lesions and microstructure, tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity.

ResultsWe replicated established case-control brain changes in Alzheimers Disease, Parkinsons Disease and Small Vessel Disease compared to healthy controls. Leveraging this joint standardised dataset, we identified distinct neuroimaging features of individual neurodegenerative disorders, providing evidence for robust diagnosis-specific brain changes. Importantly, however, there was also a large degree of transdiagnostic similarity across neuroimaging markers. Testing for transdiagnostic associations between symptoms and brain phenotypes, we found that lower medial frontal pole connectivity to primary motor cortex was preferentially associated with apathy, fatigue, and depression; whereas cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses.

ConclusionsThese results demonstrate that different neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by dissociable brain changes, but also common transdiagnostic and symptom-associated features. This suggests that shared symptoms across neurodegeneration may in part be driven by overlapping impact on key brain systems, such as changes in medial frontal pole connectivity and cingulum microstructure. Our work highlights that multimodal imaging biomarkers can help understand and parse symptomatic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative and ageing populations.

after.abstract: Organ clocks estimate the biological age of organs from blood, but current clocks assign tissue-enriched proteins to organs and train on chronological age, which requires proteomics and does not yield organ-specific disease risk. In the UK Biobank, we trained organ clocks on first onset of disease of each organ using routine laboratory tests and froze the coefficients. Under an age label, organ-clock readouts arose equally in size-matched random protein panels; with a disease label, clocks selected their own organs proteins and predicted their own organs diseases. Defining extreme aging by multiples of disease risk concentrated flags on own-organ disease. Frozen clocks kept organ correspondence in the US NHANES cohort, predicted first onset of own-organ disease in the Japanese JMDC cohort and added more information to clinical risk scores than current organ clocks. Trained once where disease follow-up exists, organ clocks can be used wherever routine laboratory tests are measured.

after.authors: Balmaceda, C.; Rios Bustamante, J. C.; Lahoz, D.; Espinoza, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Research on Health and Social Care Management (CeRGAS), Bocconi University, Milan, Italy
after.abstract:
BackgroundChilean law requires a pharmacist to direct every pharmacy throughout opening hours. Bill 18,719-11 would allow any pharmacy to replace the pharmacist with another health professional or a technician, arguing that cheaper direction would open pharmacies where there are none and lower prices. We assessed that argument and the safety consequences.

MethodsWe built a societal-perspective simulation model comparing the bill with current regulation over 2027-2036. Pharmacist hours replaced determine the share of dispensings without a pharmacist, which drives additional adverse drug reactions and therapeutic-error poisonings, estimated from national hospital discharges and published data of the national poison centre. New access in municipalities without a pharmacy was valued. The increase in errors without a pharmacist and the share of harm originating in the affected pharmacies are unmeasured and were treated as scenarios. Labour-cost savings and the net health and access value were reported separately, discounted at 3%.

ResultsIn the reference scenario, 27% of dispensings would occur without a pharmacist by 2036. Over ten years the bill would add about 2,500 admissions for adverse drug reactions, 670 poisonings from therapeutic errors (28 of them admitted) and 68 deaths (95% interval 22-166). About 17,700 people would gain a pharmacy, worth CLP 12 billion (US$13 million), against CLP 150 billion (US$165 million) in health lost and care. The net health and access value was negative in 99.9% of simulations, and with any increase in errors above 3.2%. Pharmacies would save CLP 270 billion (US$296 million) in pay, lowering medicine spending by at most 0.6-1.9% if fully passed on. A favourable economic balance would require nearly three-quarters of displaced pharmacists to be re-employed immediately at the same pay.

ConclusionsThe access and price gains are small and local, whereas the health risks would be national. They do not justify allowing every pharmacy to replace its pharmacist; access in isolated localities calls for targeted measures.

after.authors: Koross, A. K.; Morema, E. N.; Konyole, S. O.; Shisanya, M. S.
after.abstract:
BackgroundResponsive feeding -- recognising and answering a childs hunger and satiety cues without coercion -- is a World Health Organization-recommended component of complementary feeding, yet it is rarely addressed or measured in Kenyas community health system, particularly in arid and semi-arid counties.

ObjectiveTo determine whether a Community Health Promoter (CHP)-led responsive feeding intervention improves responsive feeding practices among caregivers of children aged 0-59 months in West Pokot County, Kenya, compared with usual community health services, and to evaluate its implementation.

MethodsThis is a pragmatic, two-arm, parallel-group cluster randomized controlled trial with an embedded RE-AIM mixed-methods process evaluation. Eighteen Community Health Units in two sub-counties will be randomized 1:1, stratified by sub-county, and approximately 340 caregiver-child dyads enrolled. The intervention comprises five-day competency-based CHP training, monthly household counselling and coaching visits over three months, mother-to-mother group sessions, pictorial job aids, SMS reminders and supportive supervision with fidelity assessment. The comparator is usual care. The primary outcome is the Responsive Feeding Practices Index (RFPI, 0-100), combining observed mealtime and caregiver-reported items, at three months after intervention initiation. Secondary outcomes include caregiver knowledge, attitudes and self-efficacy, minimum dietary diversity, meal frequency and age-appropriate feeding. The primary analysis is a baseline-adjusted mixed-effects linear regression with a random intercept for Community Health Unit, by intention to treat. Reach, adoption, fidelity and maintenance, with key informant interviews and focus group discussions, will be integrated by RE-AIM domain.

Ethics and disseminationThe trial is approved by the Masinde Muliro University of Science and Technology Institutional Scientific and Ethics Review Committee (MMUST/ISERC/314/2026) and licensed by the National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation (NACOSTI/P/26/4195285). Findings will be shared through publication, county feedback meetings and a policy brief.

Trial registrationPan African Clinical Trials Registry, PACTR202611787801603; registered 9 November 2026; enrolment planned from 11 January 2027.

after.title: Preprint: Structural Barriers and Socioeconomic Determinants of HIV-Related Mortality in Children Under Five: Mixed-Methods Evidence from the Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance Program, Sierra Leone
after.authors: Clumeck, S.; Rojas, C. R.; Kowuor, D.; Sesay, H. S.; Ameh, S.; Galarraga, O.; Ogbuanu, I. U.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The Africa Research Collaborative (The ARC), on behalf of the Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance
after.abstract:
AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWO_ST_ABSObjectiveC_ST_ABSDeveloping equitable prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) policies requires local evidence, yet how socioeconomic, geographic, and health system factors jointly drive HIV-related child mortality remains underexplored in Sierra Leone. This study evaluated the association between socioeconomic status (SES), geographic access, and pediatric HIV-related mortality, while examining the system-level and sociocultural barriers driving missed PMTCT opportunities.

Materials and MethodsWe used a mixed-methods design. Quantitative analyses drew on Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance Sierra Leone surveillance data (2019-2024) for deceased under five years old (U5s) with confirmed HIV status. Stepwise logistic regression evaluated associations between covariates (SES, maternal education, distance to health facilities) and a composite binary outcome of HIV-related death. Qualitatively, 33 key informant interviews with PMTCT stakeholders were analyzed using thematic framework analysis in Dedoose.

ResultsThe quantitative sample included 1,230 deceased children, of whom 162 (13.2%) reported an HIV-related death. Maternal education and distance to health facilities were statistically significant predictors of HIV-related death, whereas wealth quintiles showed no association. The qualitative findings identified system-level constraints disrupting the PMTCT cascade, including delayed entry into antenatal care, weak postnatal follow-up, stockouts of HIV test kits and antiretroviral drugs, limited polymerase chain reaction capacity and delayed results, and gaps in scheduling, tracking, and data systems. Donor-driven targets and funding constraints shaped procurement and service availability. Stigma, fear of disclosure, confidentiality concerns, transport costs, and poverty further undermined engagement and retention.

ConclusionsPediatric HIV infection and related outcomes were driven by cumulative barriers across access, service readiness, and sociocultural context rather than household wealth alone. Improving PMTCT outcomes requires strengthening diagnostic and supply chain infrastructure, enhancing patient-tracking systems, and delivering stigma-sensitive, community-anchored care.

after.title: Preprint: Institutional Distrust as the Most Frequently Reported Barrier to Health Insurance Enrollment in Post-Conflict Liberia: A Mixed-Methods Study Extending the Andersen Behavioral Model with Trust as a Fourth Enabling Resource
after.authors: Omisore, O. K.; Wollor, B.; Agala, V.; Ogaji, D. S.
after.abstract:
Health insurance enrollment in post-conflict Liberia remains below 15% despite a decade of reform, and the widely used Andersen Behavioral Model gives institutional trust no explicit place among the determinants of service use. We examined institutional distrust as a theoretically distinct barrier to enrollment using a concurrent mixed-methods design in four counties (Montserrado, Margibi, Nimba and Grand Gedeh). A cross-sectional survey of 542 adults (271 insured, 271 uninsured) ranked self-reported primary barriers and modeled enrollment with multivariable logistic regression; 16 key informant interviews and four focus group discussions, one per county, were analyzed thematically, combining deductive orientation to Andersens framework with inductive derivation of trust subtypes, and integrated with survey findings through joint display. Among uninsured respondents, institutional distrust was the most frequently reported primary barrier (57/271, 21.0%), narrowly ahead of premium cost (49, 18.1%) and inaccessibility of services (47, 17.3%), and the barrier distribution did not differ significantly by county. Four analytic subtypes were developed (fund-stewardship, benefit-delivery, provider-quality and generalized-state distrust), although direct evidence for provider-quality distrust overlapped with wider state-health-sector distrust. In multivariable analysis, socioeconomic status was the strongest structural predictor of enrollment: formal employment (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 8.78, 95% CI 4.90 to 15.76), tertiary education (aOR 8.17, 4.12 to 16.20) and secondary education (aOR 7.36, 3.98 to 13.63) each independently raised the odds of enrollment, whereas informal employment (aOR 1.35, 0.81 to 2.24), sex and county were not significant. Socioeconomic status thus structures who enrolls, while institutional distrust is the barrier the uninsured most often name, a pattern the qualitative data corroborate. We propose extending the Andersen model to treat institutional trust as a fourth enabling resource alongside financial, organizational and social-support resources. In fragile states, trust-building should be treated as health-system infrastructure that complements, rather than replaces, financial-access measures.

KEY MESSAGESO_LIAbout one in five uninsured adults in four Liberian counties named distrust of the insurance scheme as their main reason for not enrolling, slightly more than named premium cost, and the overall pattern of barriers did not differ significantly between urban, peri-urban, conflict-affected and remote counties.
C_LIO_LIDistrust is not a single attitude. Participants distinguished doubts about whether premiums are safeguarded, whether promised services are delivered, whether care under insurance is of acceptable quality, and whether the state acts in good faith; each points to a different policy lever.
C_LIO_LIEducation and formal employment remain the strongest predictors of who holds insurance, so trust-building must accompany, not substitute for, measures that lower financial and access barriers for informal-sector households.
C_LIO_LIEnrollment strategies in fragile and post-conflict states should budget for trust-building as health-system infrastructure: ring-fenced and audited funds, published benefit guarantees, responsive grievance redress, quality monitoring and inclusive oversight, and studies using the Andersen model should measure institutional trust as an enabling resource.
C_LI

Reflexivity statementThe author team comprises public health and health systems researchers based at Nigerian institutions and a Liberia-based co-author: the first author is a doctoral researcher at the University of Port Harcourt, one co-author is based at a medical center in Liberia and facilitated field access, and the other co-authors bring experience from a state contributory health insurance program (RIVCHPP) and a university center of excellence in public health research. With most of the team working from Nigerian institutional bases, the team was attentive to the risk of importing assumptions from the Nigerian insurance context. Experience within the team of insurance program administration may have sensitized the analysis to scheme design and stewardship concerns. To examine how these positions shaped interpretation, the lead analyst kept reflexive memos throughout coding, community leaders were consulted on instrument wording, and preliminary findings were presented back to community focus groups in each study county before manuscript preparation.

Ethical approvalEthical approval was granted by the Research Ethics Committee of the University of Port Harcourt (December 2024; reference UPH/CEREMAD/REC/MM105/030). A letter of local institutional support for data collection in Liberia was obtained (May 2026). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Funding, acknowledgements, conflicts of interest and author contributions are given in the Declarations section.

Here, we performed deep long-read direct RNA sequencing on human frontal cortex from six AD cases and six controls to characterize native mRNA modifications transcriptome-wide and across AD-relevant genes. We evaluated differential nucleotide modifications between cases and controls transcriptome-wide, and we then performed two association tests within APOE: (1) associations between mRNA modifications and rs429358 alleles in five {epsilon}3/{epsilon}4 heterozygotes; and (2) pairwise associations between co-occurring mRNA modifications. We identified four modifications associated with rs429358--all within 15 nucleotides of the SNP. Among them was an N6-methyladenosine (m6A) located at chr19:44,908,679 (OR = 0.53; p = 1.4x10-109)--five nucleotides upstream of rs429358--that was 14.5 percentage points lower on {epsilon}4-derived mRNA (27.7%) compared to {epsilon}3 (42.2%). This directional difference was observed within each individual, supporting a consistent allele-associated modification pattern (p = 4.2x10-5). We also identified 344 associations among 73 APOE modifications, suggesting a potentially complex, coordinated network of mRNA biological signals within APOE, alone. Our findings suggest that mRNA modifications may contribute to APOE-associated risk, though validation in large independent cohorts and functional experiments will be necessary to determine the biological consequences of these associations and their potential relevance to AD pathogenesis. Together, our findings highlight the potential of allele-resolved direct RNA sequencing to characterize genetic associations with RNA modifications at a major AD risk locus.

after.authors: Omisore, O. K.; Wollor, B.; Agala, V.; Ogaji, D. S.
after.abstract: Health insurance enrollment in post-conflict Liberia remains below 15% despite a decade of reform, and the widely used Andersen Behavioral Model gives institutional trust no explicit place among the determinants of service use. We examined institutional distrust as a theoretically distinct barrier to enrollment using a concurrent mixed-methods design in four counties (Montserrado, Margibi, Nimba and Grand Gedeh). A cross-sectional survey of 542 adults (271 insured, 271 uninsured) ranked self-reported primary barriers and modeled enrollment with multivariable logistic regression; 16 key informant interviews and four focus group discussions, one per county, were analyzed thematically, combining deductive orientation to Andersen's framework with inductive derivation of trust subtypes, and integrated with survey findings through joint display. Among uninsured respondents, institutional distrust was the most frequently reported primary barrier (57/271, 21.0%), narrowly ahead of premium cost (49, 18.1%) and inaccessibility of services (47, 17.3%), and the barrier distribution did not differ significantly by county. Four analytic subtypes were developed (fund-stewardship, benefit-delivery, provider-quality and generalized-state distrust), although direct evidence for provider-quality distrust overlapped with wider state-health-sector distrust. In multivariable analysis, socioeconomic status was the strongest structural predictor of enrollment: formal employment (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 8.78, 95% CI 4.90 to 15.76), tertiary education (aOR 8.17, 4.12 to 16.20) and secondary education (aOR 7.36, 3.98 to 13.63) each independently raised the odds of enrollment, whereas informal employment (aOR 1.35, 0.81 to 2.24), sex and county were not significant. Socioeconomic status thus structures who enrolls, while institutional distrust is the barrier the uninsured most often name, a pattern the qualitative data corroborate. We propose extending the Andersen model to treat institutional trust as a fourth enabling resource alongside financial, organizational and social-support resources. In fragile states, trust-building should be treated as health-system infrastructure that complements, rather than replaces, financial-access measures.

after.title: Preprint: Integrated Stepped-Care Task-Shared Intervention for Depression Symptoms in Older Adults Living with HIV in Nigeria: A pilot randomized controlled study
after.authors: Elugbadebo, O. O.; Akintade, F. M.; Omoloye, T. T.; Oladeji, B. D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry, College of Medicine, University of Ibadan, Oyo
after.abstract: **Background** Depression can affect treatment adherence and quality of life of older adults living with HIV, yet evidence on integrated stepped-care task-shared (SCT) interventions in African settings remains limited. We assessed the feasibility of an adapted SCT intervention among adults aged >=50 years receiving HIV care in Ibadan, Nigeria and examined preliminary differences in depressive symptoms, quality of life and ART adherence. **Methods** This was a two-arm, parallel-group, randomised pilot superiority trial embedded in a mixed-methods effectiveness-implementation study in Ibadan, Nigeria. Adults aged >=50 years living with HIV and scoring >=10 on the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) were randomised (1:1) to stepped-care task-sharing (SCT; n=50) or treatment as usual (TAU; n=50). SCT involved psychosocial sessions delivered by trained HIV clinic providers, with antidepressant treatment and specialist review according to depression severity and treatment response. TAU involved routine HIV care and referral to a separate psychiatric clinic. Outcomes were assessed at six weeks, three months and six months by assessors blinded to allocation. Feasibility indicators included recruitment, retention and intervention delivery. Preliminary clinical effectiveness was assessed using mixed-effects models for PHQ-9, quality of life (WHOQOL-HIV BREF) and ART adherence (Simplified Medication Adherence Questionnaire). Analyses followed randomised allocation using Stata/MP 15. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06894680). **Results** Of the 757 participants screened, 120 participants were eligible and 100 (83.3%) were randomised, with 50 allocated to the SCT and 50 to TAU. All 50 SCT participants received the first psychosocial session, 40 (80%) attended at least two sessions and 30 (60%) completed all six sessions. Of 23 participants prescribed antidepressants, five (21.7%) initiated treatment. Baseline mean PHQ-9 scores were 13.24 (SD 4.43) in SCT and 14.12 (SD 4.48) in TAU. Of the 17 participants in TAU referred to the UCH psychiatric clinic, one attended but subsequently disengaged from care. Adjusted between-group differences (TAU minus SCT) favoured SCT at six weeks (3.95 points, 95% CI 1.91-5.99; p<0.001), three months (3.66, 95% CI 1.60-5.71; p<0.001) and six months (3.15, 95% CI 1.09-5.20; p=0.003). Quality-of-life scores increased in both groups, with no significant between-group differences at baseline, 3 months, or 6 months (all p>0.05). Differences in quality of life and ART adherence were not statistically significant. No adverse events were recorded. **Conclusion** This pilot trial demonstrated that the recruitment, retention and psychosocial SCT delivery were feasible within routine HIV care. SCT showed promising reductions in depressive symptoms over six months, although antidepressant initiation was limited. Further multisite evaluation should examine clinical effectiveness, intervention fidelity and implementation outcomes.

after.authors: Zhang, M.; Song, X.; Pan, Z.; Wan, M.; Song, Z.; Li, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The First Affiliated Hospital of Army Medical University (Southwest Hospital)
after.abstract: Background: Persistent facial erythema and episodic flushing are prominent features of erythematotelangiectatic rosacea (ETR). The efficacy of auricular acupuncture (AA) for ETR is uncertain. Methods: This multicenter, randomized, participant- and assessor-masked, sham-controlled superiority trial was designed to enroll 108 adults aged 18 to 50 years with ETR and a baseline Clinician Erythema Assessment (CEA) score of at least 2 at 5 hospitals in China. Participants were allocated 1:1 to AA with semipermanent intradermal needles or visually matched, same-site nonpenetrating sham stimulation. Four auricular points (Shenmen, Sanjiao, Endocrine, and Heart) were treated on alternating ears every 3 days for 6 weeks, with self-pressure 3 times daily. Follow-up was scheduled through week 10. The primary outcome was clinician-rated erythema (CEA score) at week 6. Secondary outcomes comprised other clinician-rated erythema assessments, patient-rated redness, flushing, migraine symptoms, sleep quality, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and adverse events. The primary treatment contrast was planned using baseline-adjusted analysis of covariance with multiple imputation for missing week 6 outcomes. Secondary longitudinal outcomes were planned for exploratory mixed-model analyses. Discussion: The trial was designed to assess the incremental efficacy and tolerability of penetrating auricular needling compared with a matched nonpenetrating procedure. Same-site pressure in both groups may have physiological effects, which should be considered when interpreting the results.

after.authors: Shi, C.; Sun, Y.; Ruan, X.; Shi, R.; Yao, C.; Zhou, H.; Xu, X.; Li, X.; Na, R.
after.abstract: Organ clocks estimate the biological age of organs from blood, but current clocks assign tissue-enriched proteins to organs and train on chronological age, which requires proteomics and does not yield organ-specific disease risk. In the UK Biobank, we trained organ clocks on first onset of disease of each organ using routine laboratory tests and froze the coefficients. Under an age label, organ-clock readouts arose equally in size-matched random protein panels; with a disease label, clocks selected their own organ's proteins and predicted their own organ's diseases. Defining extreme aging by multiples of disease risk concentrated flags on own-organ disease. Frozen clocks kept organ correspondence in the US NHANES cohort, predicted first onset of own-organ disease in the Japanese JMDC cohort and added more information to clinical risk scores than current organ clocks. Trained once where disease follow-up exists, organ clocks can be used wherever routine laboratory tests are measured.

after.authors: Balmaceda, C.; Rios Bustamante, J. C.; Lahoz, D.; Espinoza, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Research on Health and Social Care Management (CeRGAS), Bocconi University, Milan, Italy
after.abstract: Background Chilean law requires a pharmacist to direct every pharmacy throughout opening hours. Bill 18,719-11 would allow any pharmacy to replace the pharmacist with another health professional or a technician, arguing that cheaper direction would open pharmacies where there are none and lower prices. We assessed that argument and the safety consequences. Methods We built a societal-perspective simulation model comparing the bill with current regulation over 2027-2036. Pharmacist hours replaced determine the share of dispensings without a pharmacist, which drives additional adverse drug reactions and therapeutic-error poisonings, estimated from national hospital discharges and published data of the national poison centre. New access in municipalities without a pharmacy was valued. The increase in errors without a pharmacist and the share of harm originating in the affected pharmacies are unmeasured and were treated as scenarios. Labour-cost savings and the net health and access value were reported separately, discounted at 3%. Results In the reference scenario, 27% of dispensings would occur without a pharmacist by 2036. Over ten years the bill would add about 2,500 admissions for adverse drug reactions, 670 poisonings from therapeutic errors (28 of them admitted) and 68 deaths (95% interval 22-166). About 17,700 people would gain a pharmacy, worth CLP 12 billion (US$13 million), against CLP 150 billion (US$165 million) in health lost and care. The net health and access value was negative in 99.9% of simulations, and with any increase in errors above 3.2%. Pharmacies would save CLP 270 billion (US$296 million) in pay, lowering medicine spending by at most 0.6-1.9% if fully passed on. A favourable economic balance would require nearly three-quarters of displaced pharmacists to be re-employed immediately at the same pay. Conclusions The access and price gains are small and local, whereas the health risks would be national. They do not justify allowing every pharmacy to replace its pharmacist; access in isolated localities calls for targeted measures.

after.authors: Pereira Neves, H.; Dias Guimaraes, A. R.; Leao dos Santos, J. F.; Martins Magnus, M.; Ribeiro Silva, V.; Bandeira da Silva, R.; Sobreira Messias, G.; Ferreira, W. E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Rene Rachou Institute, Oswaldo Cruz Foundation; Lucas Machado Educational Foundation
after.abstract: Background Amoebic liver abscess, caused by Entamoeba histolytica, is a potential life threatening extra intestinal infection that is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Entamoeba histolytica is morphologically indistinguishable from the non-pathogenic Entamoeba dispar, yet species-level confirmation is critical before initiating metronidazole. This is particularly important in elderly patients, for whom the drug carries a higher risk of QT prolongation, peripheral neuropathy, and hepatotoxicity. In Brazil, where E. dispar predominates over E. histolytica at an estimated 10:1 ratio, diagnostic misidentification constitutes a genuine hazard. Methodology and Principal Findings We report a patient with amoebic liver abscess with secondary hepatic biochemical derangement requiring urgent molecular species confirmation. A Nucleic Acid Sequence- Based Amplification (NASBA) assay was designed targeting a species-specific region of the E. histolytica 40S small subunit ribosomal RNA (GenBank MW026793.1). Primer design using NCBI Primer-BLAST yielded a thermodynamically balanced primer pair, with melting temperatures of 53.25{degrees}C and 53.81{degrees}C and a resulting amplicon with 121 nucleotides, which is suitable for standard NASBA at 41{degrees}C. Applied to an aspirated abscess sample, the assay returned a positive result confirming E. histolytica infection and enabling continuation of antiamoebic therapy with favourable clinical outcome. Conclusions and Significance NASBA targeting E. histolytica small subunit ribosomal RNA provides species-specific diagnosis through two orthogonal mechanisms: sequence-level discrimination from E. dispar at the primer binding sites, and the intrinsic viability bias or RNA amplification, which favours signal from metabolically active trophozoites over residual nucleic acid. The episomal architecture of E. histolytica ribosomal DNA, which has approximately 200 extrachromosomal gene copies per trophozoite (each actively transcribed), confers inherent sensitivity amplification. Operating isothermally at 41{degrees}C without a thermocycler or any additional laboratory infrastructure, this approach addresses a genuine diagnostic gap in neglected tropical disease management and is suited to point-of-care deployment in resource-limited endemic settings.

after.abstract: Background: Achromobacter are a genus of difficult-to-treat, frequently multi-drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria that can cause severe infections in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Bacteriophages are an understudied yet promising therapy for these and other antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, data are largely limited to case reports or series, and clinical trials among pwCF to date have not evaluated Achromobacter. Methods: This is an investigator-initiated, open-label, randomized phase 1 pilot trial to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and biological effects of AchromoPhage, a cocktail of four genetically distinct, obligately lytic Achromobacter-targeting phages (phiACH01, phiACH04, phiACH06, phiACH07) with broad activity against Achromobacter species, in 12 adult participants with CF and pulmonary Achromobacter infection. Twelve participants will be randomized into three groups to receive a total of three, increasing, weekly doses of the AchromoPhage cocktail via one of three routes: 1) intravenous, 2) via inhalation, or 3) or intravenously and inhaled. Participation in the trial will span approximately 7 weeks, which will consist of outpatient phage dose administrations, safety and symptom monitoring, and longitudinal collection of biospecimens for protocol-specified and exploratory analyses through Day 42. The primary safety endpoint is the occurrence of treatment-related Grade 4 or greater adverse events. Secondary endpoints include longitudinal changes in FEV1 by spirometry, longitudinal changes in health-related quality of life, pharmacokinetics of each of the four phages in blood and the respiratory tract, and emergence of a phage neutralizing antibody response in serum. Discussion: While existing case anecdotes and observational studies suggest that phages are safe and may have a role in treating human infections, there is a paucity of clinical trials studying the adverse effect profile and basic pharmacological parameters of phages. This trial will study the safety and explore the pharmacokinetic and other properties of a four-phage cocktail in patients with CF and chronic Achromobacter lung infection. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT0727590. Registered on 12/10/2025

after.title: Preprint: Equity gaps in the genetic diagnosis of monogenic cardiomyopathy: an intersectional analysis of race and gender in the All of Us Research Program
after.authors: Theberge, E. T.; Anderson, S. J.; Lehman, A. M.
after.abstract: Purpose: Diagnostic yield from genetic testing in cardiomyopathy depends on reference data and access to care, which differ by race and gender, yet are rarely studied jointly. Methods: We analyzed 414,830 genome-sequenced All of Us participants for predicted deleterious variants (PDVs) in 58 cardiomyopathy genes, comparing ClinVar classifications by race and modelling cardiac outcomes against matched controls and, within heterozygotes, by race and gender. Among GLA or TTR pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) carriers with cardiomyopathy, we explored Fabry disease or amyloidosis diagnosis codes by race, gender, income and education. Results: PDVs in White participants were more often P/LP (13.9% vs 12.0%, p<0.001), more so among heterozygotes with cardiomyopathy (29.6% vs 22.1%, p=0.004). Cardiomyopathy odds rose from missense to loss-of-function PDVs (OR 1.12-1.79). Twenty of 131 GLA/TTR P/LP carriers with cardiomyopathy had a syndromic code; White women had higher odds than non-White women (OR 6.50, 95% CI 1.35-31.34). Syndromic codes were nominally associated with higher income and education, and 47 of 48 carriers with income <$25k were non-White. Conclusion: Variant classification and syndromic diagnosis are less complete for non-White carriers, particularly women. Equitable precision cardiology requires more diverse reference data and analyses that treat race and gender as effect modifiers.
